The Tuṣita devaputras, the Nirmāṇarati devaputras, the Paranirmitavaśavartin devaputras, the Brahmakāyika devas, the Brahmapurohita devas, the Brahmapārṣadya devas, the Mahābrahmāṇa devas, the Ābhā devas, the Parīttābhā devas, the Apramāṇābhā devas, the Ābhāsvara devas, the Śubha devas, the Parīttaśubha devas, and the Apramāṇaśubha devas.
The Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Bṛha gods, the Parīttabṛha gods, the Apramāṇabṛha gods, the Bṛhatphala gods,

the Abṛha gods, the Atapa gods, the Sudṛśa gods, the Sudarśana gods, and the Akaniṣṭha gods will constantly and perpetually provide protection, defense, and guardianship for those sons of good family and daughters of good family.
Those sons of the gods who, having come, shall honor, revere, respect, and worship this Perfection of Wisdom after it has been written down and preserved—
Kauśika, for anyone who writes down and preserves this Perfection of Wisdom, these [benefits] will be his in this very life.

There will be these qualities and benefits. For example, Kauśika, whatever beings—whether animals or humans—who have gone to the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), or are in its vicinity, or within the seat of awakening, cannot be harassed or harmed by either a human or a non-human. Why is that?

For it was here that those former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones sat and fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. And those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones who will appear in the future time, they too shall sit right here and fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who currently reside in the world systems in the ten directions— they too, having sat right here, have fully awakened to unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment. By all those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas...
Having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, he has practiced for the sake of the fearlessness, freedom from enmity, and freedom from exhaustion of all sentient beings;
thus immeasurable and incalculable beings have been established, will be established, and are being established in the excellences of gods and humans,
and they have been established, will be established, and are being established in the fruit of stream-entry.

They have been established, will be established, and are being established in the fruit of once-returning; they have been established, will be established, and are being established in the fruit of non-returning; they have been established, will be established, and are being established in arhatship.
They have been established, will be established, and are being established in pratyekabodhi. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, by means of this very perfection of wisdom, that spot of earth is made into a shrine for all beings;
it is to be saluted, revered, honored, worshipped, respected, and esteemed with flowers, incense, and so forth.
With garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags.
Śakra said: "Blessed One, whichever son of good family or daughter of good family..."

Having written down this perfection of wisdom and made it into a book, you should preserve it; and you should honor, revere, respect, and worship it with flowers, incense, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags.
And [you should do so] for the relics of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, who has entered final nirvāṇa, within a stūpa made of the seven precious gems.
One should establish or preserve them, having fashioned them out of the seven precious gems and raised aloft;
and one should honor, revere, and worship them with flowers, incense, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags.
"Which of these two would produce the greater mass of merit?
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, Kauśika, I shall question you on this very point."
Answer as you see fit. What do you think, Kauśika:

regarding this omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) attained by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and this physical body (*ātmabhāva*) that has been manifested—training in which practice did the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One [attain them]?
"Having attained omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), this very personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) was brought forth.

Śakra said: "It is right here, Blessed One, while training in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, attained omniscience and brought forth this very personal existence.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Kauśika, so it is!
While training here in the perfection of wisdom, I attained omniscience and brought forth this very body."

It is not by means of this acquisition of a physical body, Kauśika, that the Tathāgata is reckoned as "Tathāgata. Rather, it is by the acquisition of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) that the Tathāgata is reckoned as "Tathāgata.
And this knowledge of all aspects, Kauśika, has issued forth from the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Thus, Kauśika, this physical body is the basis for that knowledge of the omniscience of all aspects; and by relying upon this basis, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha attained the omniscience of all aspects. In this way, this physical body, as the basis for that knowledge of the omniscience of all aspects, has become a shrine for all sentient beings—a body to be saluted, honored, worshipped, and revered.
Kauśika, even when he has entered final nirvāṇa, the relics shall be treated with reverence, and thus there will be worship of the body,
but not otherwise through the worship of the Dharma. For any son of good family or daughter of good family, Kauśika, who writes down this perfection of wisdom,
and takes it up, bears it in mind, recites it, masters it, and attends to it with proper mental attention—
He will honor, revere, respect, and worship it with flowers, incense, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags;
by him, an act of worship toward the knowledge of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatājñāna*) will have been performed. Therefore, Kausika, a faithful son of good family...

Or, a son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to worship the Tathāgata should write down this very Perfection of Wisdom, and it should be taken up, retained, recited, mastered, and properly attended to;
it should be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped with flowers, incense, garlands, and perfumes.

With ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags; and whoever, Kauśika, after the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa, should establish his relics in stupas made of the seven precious gems,
or having placed them in a casket made of the seven precious gems, should carry them about, and then honor, revere, and respect them.

One should worship with flowers, incense, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags; and whoever, having written down this *prajñāpāramitā*, should take it up, bear it, recite it, master it,
and attend to it properly, and should honor, revere, respect, and worship it with flowers and incense— [that person would generate greater merit].
With garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags—this very person would generate a much greater mass of merit than that. Why is that?
For it is from this, Kauśika, that the five perfections emerge.
From this they emerge as internal emptiness; from this they emerge as external emptiness;
from this they emerge as internal-external emptiness.
From this, the emptiness of emptiness emerges;
from this, the great emptiness emerges;
from this, the emptiness of the ultimate truth emerges.
From this, conditioned emptiness emerges;
from this, unconditioned emptiness emerges;
from this, absolute emptiness emerges.
From this, the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end is derived;
from this, the emptiness of non-dispersal is derived;
from this, the emptiness of intrinsic nature is derived.
From this, the emptiness of all phenomena emerges;
from this, the emptiness of specific characteristics emerges;
from this, the emptiness of non-apprehension emerges.
From this, the emptiness of non-existence emerges; from this, the emptiness of intrinsic nature emerges; from this, the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence emerges.
From this, the four foundations of mindfulness emerge;
from this, the four right efforts emerge;
from this, the four bases of psychic power emerge.
From this the five faculties emerge;
from this the five powers emerge;
from this the seven factors of enlightenment emerge.
From this the noble eightfold path emerges; from this the four noble truths emerge;
from this the four meditative absorptions emerge.
From this, the four immeasurables emerge;
from this, the four formless attainments emerge;
from this, the eight liberations emerge.
From this emerge the nine successive meditative attainments;
from this emerge the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
from this emerge the five supernormal powers.
From this all samādhis emerge; from this all dhāraṇī-doors emerge;
from this the ten powers of a Tathāgata emerge.
From this, the four grounds of self-confidence emerge;
from this, the four analytical knowledges emerge;
from this, great compassion emerges.
From this emerge the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; from this emerges the ripening of sentient beings; from this emerges the perfection of the Buddha-field.
From this proceeds the excellence of family of the bodhisattva mahāsattva; from this proceeds the excellence of physical form;
from this proceeds the excellence of gain.
From this arises the perfection of the retinue; from this arises great loving-kindness;
from this arises great compassion.
From this [Dharma] have emerged the great noble families of kṣatriyas; from this have emerged the great noble families of brāhmaṇas; from this have emerged the great noble families of householders.
From this [Dharma] emerged the sons of the gods belonging to the retinue of the Four Great Kings;
from this emerged the sons of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three; from this emerged the sons of the Yāma gods.
From this [Dharma] have the Tuṣita sons of gods emerged; from this have the Nirmāṇarati sons of gods emerged;
from this have the Paranirmitavaśavartin sons of gods emerged.
From this [Dharma] have emerged the sons of the gods belonging to the Brahmakāyika realm; from this have emerged the sons of the gods belonging to the Brahmapurohita realm;
from this have emerged the sons of the gods belonging to the Brahmapārṣadya realm.
From this emerge the Mahābrahmāṇa sons of the gods; from this emerge the Ābhā gods;
from this emerge the Parīttābhā gods.
From this, the gods of Immeasurable Light emerged;
from this, the gods of Utmost Light emerged;
from this, the gods of Purity emerged.
From this, the Parīttaśubha gods have emerged;
from this, the Apramāṇaśubha gods have emerged;
from this, the Śubhakṛtsna gods have emerged.
From this, the Bṛhat devas have emerged; from this, the Parīttabṛhat devas have emerged; from this, the Apramāṇabṛhat devas have emerged.
From this, the Bṛhatphala gods have emerged;
from this, the Abṛha gods have emerged;
from this, the Atapa gods have emerged.
From this, the Sudṛśa gods have emerged;
from this, the Sudarśana gods have emerged; from this, the Akaniṣṭha gods have emerged.
From this they have emerged as stream-enterers;
from this they have emerged as once-returners;
from this they have emerged as non-returners.
From this [perfection] the Arhats have emerged;
from this the Pratyekabuddhas have emerged; from this the Bodhisattvas have emerged.
From this, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have emerged;
from this, the omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas has emerged.

Śakra said: "Blessed One, these humans of Jambudvīpa do not honor, revere, respect, or worship this perfection of wisdom. Is it, then, that these humans of Jambudvīpa do not know at all that great power results from making offerings to the perfection of wisdom?"

The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Kauśika? Among these humans of Jambudvīpa, who are endowed with unbreakable faith in the Buddha, who are endowed with unbreakable faith in the Dharma, and who are endowed with unbreakable faith in the Saṃgha;
who are free from doubt regarding the Buddha, free from doubt regarding the Dharma, and free from doubt regarding the Saṃgha—"
"Those who have reached certainty in the Buddha, who have reached certainty in the Dharma, and who have reached certainty in the Saṃgha.
Śakra said: "Blessed One, those humans of Jambudvīpa who are endowed with an unbreakable faith in the Buddha are few."

Those who are endowed with unbreakable faith in the Dharma; those who are endowed with unbreakable faith in the Saṅgha; those who are free from doubt regarding the Buddha, free from doubt regarding the Dharma, and free from doubt regarding the Saṅgha;
those who have reached certainty regarding the Buddha, reached certainty regarding the Dharma, and reached certainty regarding the Saṅgha.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Kauśika? How many are those humans of Jambudvīpa who are attainers of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment?"
How many are those Jambudvīpa humans who have attained the three gateways to liberation?
How many are those Jambudvīpa humans who have attained the eight liberations? How many are those Jambudvīpa humans who have attained the nine successive meditative attainments?
How many are those Jambudvīpa humans who have attained the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid)?
How many are those Jambudvīpa humans who have attained the six superknowledges (abhijñā)?
How many are those Jambudvīpa humans who, through the abandonment of the three fetters (saṃyojana), have become stream-enterers (srotaāpanna)?
How many are those Jambudvīpa humans who, by the thinning of passion, hatred, and delusion, are once-returners;
how many are those Jambudvīpa humans who, through the abandonment of the five lower fetters, are non-returners;
and how many are those Jambudvīpa humans who, through the abandonment of the five higher fetters, are arhats?

"How many of those humans in Jambudvīpa have set out for the awakening of a pratyekabuddha? How many of those humans in Jambudvīpa have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening? Śakra replied: "Blessed One, those beings in Jambudvīpa who have attained the thirty-seven factors of awakening are few; even fewer than they are those who have attained the three gateways to liberation."
There are fewer who have attained the eight gates of liberation; fewer still who have attained the successive meditative absorptions;
fewer still who have attained the four analytical knowledges; and fewer still who have attained the six supernormal powers.
Among those humans of Jambudvīpa, few are those who, through the abandonment of the three fetters, have become stream-enterers;

fewer still are those who, through the attenuation of passion, hatred, and delusion, have become once-returners; fewer still are those who, through the abandonment of the five fetters conducive to immovability, have become non-returners; and fewer still are those who [have abandoned] the five fetters conducive to the peaks.

Compared to those who have abandoned [defilements] and become arhats, there are even fewer people among the inhabitants of Jambudvīpa who have set out for the awakening of a pratyekabuddha; and there are even fewer people among the inhabitants of Jambudvīpa who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
The Blessed One said:

"So it is, Kauśika, so it is! Those Jambudvīpa humans who are endowed with unbreakable faith in the Buddha are few; those who are endowed with unbreakable faith in the Dharma are few; and those who are endowed with unbreakable faith in the Saṅgha are few."
Even fewer than those are they who are free from doubt regarding the Buddha, free from doubt regarding the Dharma, and free from doubt regarding the Saṃgha;

even fewer than those are they who have reached certainty regarding the Buddha, reached certainty regarding the Dharma, and reached certainty regarding the Saṃgha; and even fewer than those among the humans of Jambudvīpa are they who have attained the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.

There are fewer who have entered the stream; fewer still who are once-returners; fewer still who are non-returners; fewer still who are arhats; fewer still who have set out for pratyekabuddha-enlightenment;
fewer still who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and fewer still who are [actually] established in enlightenment.
They wander about. For what reason?

Because in the past, while wandering through saṃsāra, they did not see a Buddha, they did not hear the Dharma, they did not attend upon the Saṅgha, they did not give gifts, they did not maintain ethical discipline, they did not cultivate patience, they did not exert vigor, and they did not practice the meditative concentrations.
Wisdom was not cultivated; the perfection of generosity was neither heard nor cultivated;
the perfection of ethical discipline was neither heard nor cultivated.
The perfection of patience was neither heard nor cultivated;
the perfection of vigor was neither heard nor cultivated;
the perfection of meditation was neither heard nor cultivated.
The perfection of wisdom has not been heard, nor has it been cultivated.
Internal emptiness has not been heard, nor has it been cultivated;
external emptiness has not been heard, nor has it been cultivated.
Internal-and-external emptiness has not been heard and not been cultivated;
the emptiness of emptiness has not been heard and not been cultivated;
great emptiness has not been heard and not been cultivated.
Ultimate emptiness has not been heard and has not been cultivated;
conditioned emptiness has not been heard and has not been cultivated;
unconditioned emptiness has not been heard and has not been cultivated.
The emptiness of the ultimate has not been heard, nor has it been cultivated;
the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end has not been heard, nor has it been cultivated;
the emptiness of non-dispersal has not been heard, nor has it been cultivated.
They have neither heard nor cultivated the emptiness of intrinsic nature;
they have neither heard nor cultivated the emptiness of all phenomena; they have neither heard nor cultivated the emptiness of specific characteristics.
Non-apprehension emptiness has not been heard and has not been cultivated;
non-existence emptiness has not been heard and has not been cultivated.
The emptiness of intrinsic nature has not been heard, nor has it been cultivated;
the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence has not been heard, nor has it been cultivated.
The applications of mindfulness have not been heard, nor have they been cultivated.
The right efforts have not been heard of nor cultivated;
the bases of psychic power have not been heard of nor cultivated;
the faculties have not been heard of nor cultivated.
The powers have not been heard of nor cultivated;
the factors of enlightenment have not been heard of nor cultivated; the noble eightfold path has not been heard of nor cultivated.
The noble truths have not been heard, nor have they been cultivated; the meditative absorptions have not been heard, nor have they been cultivated;
the immeasurables have not been heard, nor have they been cultivated.
The formless attainments have not been heard of nor cultivated;
the eight liberations have not been heard of nor cultivated; the serial attainments of meditative dwelling have not been heard of nor cultivated.
The gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—have not been heard of nor cultivated;
the superknowledges have not been heard of nor cultivated;
the meditative concentrations have not been heard of nor cultivated.
The gateways of dhāraṇī have not been heard and have not been cultivated;
the powers of a Tathāgata have not been heard and have not been cultivated;
the grounds of self-confidence have not been heard and have not been cultivated.
The analytical knowledges have not been heard nor cultivated;
great compassion has not been heard nor cultivated;
the unique qualities of a Buddha have not been heard nor cultivated.
Omniscience has not been heard and has not been cultivated;
the knowledge of the aspects of the path has not been heard and has not been cultivated;
the knowledge of all aspects has not been heard and has not been cultivated.
Therefore, Kauśika, by this method you should understand it thus:
those beings of Jambudvīpa who are endowed with unbreakable faith in the Buddha, endowed with unbreakable faith in the Dharma, and endowed with unbreakable faith in the Saṅgha are few;
even fewer than those are they who have attained the three gates of liberation.
Fewer still are those who have attained the eight liberations; fewer still are those who have attained the nine successive meditative attainments;
and fewer still are those who have attained the four analytical knowledges.
Even fewer than those are they who have attained the six supernormal powers; even fewer than those are the humans of Jambudvīpa who, through the abandonment of the three fetters, are stream-enterers;

even fewer than those are the once-returners who, through the attenuation of passion, hatred, and delusion, are once-returners; and even fewer than those are the non-returners who, through the abandonment of the five lower fetters, are non-returners.

Fewer still are those who, through the abandonment of the five higher fetters, have become arhats; fewer still than those are the humans of Jambudvīpa who have set out for the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; and fewer still than those are they who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Then, those who practice for the sake of awakening with a resolute intention are even fewer still; let alone humans, Kauśika. What do you think, Kauśika: how many living beings in Jambudvīpa are there who have attained the thirty-seven factors of awakening, who have attained the three gateways to liberation, who have attained the eight gateways to liberation, or who have attained the nine [gateways]...?

Those who have attained the successive meditative absorptions, those who have attained the four analytical knowledges, and those who have attained the six superknowledges—how many such beings are there in Jambudvīpa who, through the abandonment of the three fetters, are stream-enterers; who, through the attenuation of passion, hatred, and delusion, are once-returners; and who, through the abandonment of the five lower fetters, are non-returners?
Those who, through the abandonment of the five higher fetters, have become Arhats;

those who have set out for Pratyekabuddha-enlightenment—how many living beings in Jambudvīpa are there who are free from doubt regarding unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, and free from doubt regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha? How many such beings are there in Jambudvīpa?

Those living beings who recognize their mother, who recognize their father, who are devoted to the ascetic life, who show honor to their elders in the family, who give gifts, who guard their moral conduct, who observe the fast of patience and the poṣadha, and who dwell perceiving [all things] as wood and so forth— [they do not fall].

Among those beings of Jambudvīpa who possess the perception of impermanence, the perception of non-self, the perception of impurity, and the perception of lack of delight in all worlds— how many of them have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?

Śakra said: "O Blessed One, those living beings in Jambudvīpa who have attained the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are few; those who have attained the three gateways to liberation are few; and those who have attained the eight liberations are few."
Those who have attained the nine successive meditative attainments,
those who have attained the four analytical knowledges,
and those who have attained the six supernormal powers;
Those who, through the abandonment of the three fetters, are stream-enterers;
those who, through the attenuation of passion, hatred, and delusion, are once-returners;
and those who, through the abandonment of the five lower fetters, are non-returners.

“Those who are Arhats through the abandonment of the five higher fetters, and those who have set out for Pratyekabuddha-enlightenment—these are few, O Blessed One. Even fewer than those are the living beings in Jambudvīpa who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Kauśika, so it is! It is just as you say.
Few indeed, Kauśika, are those beings in Jambudvīpa who have attained the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment."
Those who have attained the three gates of liberation,
those who have attained the eight liberations,
those who have attained the nine successive meditative attainments, those who have attained the four analytical knowledges, and those who have attained the six supernormal powers;
Those who, through the abandonment of the three fetters, are stream-enterers;
those who, through the attenuation of passion, hatred, and delusion, are once-returners;
those who, through the abandonment of the five lower fetters, are non-returners; and those who, through the abandonment of the five higher fetters, are arhats.

Those who have set out for the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, and those who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment— of these, those who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment are fewer still.
They practice; therefore, those who desire to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment are even fewer than that.

Here, Kauśika, with my unobstructed Buddha-eye, I see in the eastern direction—in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā—immeasurable and incalculable beings who, being devoid of skillful means and the perfection of wisdom regarding unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, have for the most part established themselves on the level of a Śrāvaka or the level of a Pratyekabuddha, while only one or two have been established on the stage of non-retrogression.
Or they remain [in that state]. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is difficult to realize for those who are indolent, lacking in vigor, deficient in resolve, and lacking in wisdom.

"Here, Kauśika, with my unobstructed Buddha-eye, I see in the southern direction, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, immeasurable and incalculable beings who, being devoid of the skillful means of the perfection of wisdom for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, only one or two among them become established in the stage of non-retrogression, while the vast majority remain on the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha. For what reason is that?"
For, Kauśika, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is indeed difficult to realize for those who are indolent,

lacking in vigor, deficient in resolve, and lacking in wisdom. Here, Kauśika, with my unobstructed Buddha-eye, I see in the western direction, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, immeasurable and incalculable beings [established] for unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.

Those who lack the perfection of wisdom and skill in means—only one or two among them will be established on the stage of non-retrogression; for the most part, they remain on the stage of a śrāvaka or the stage of a pratyekabuddha. For what reason? Because, Kauśika, supreme perfect enlightenment is difficult to realize.

"By those who are indolent, lacking in vigor, possessing inferior resolve, and lacking in wisdom. Here, Kauśika, with my unobstructed Buddha-eye, I see in the northern direction, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, immeasurable and incalculable beings who, being devoid of the perfection of wisdom and skill in means directed toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, have for the most part established themselves on the level of a Śrāvaka or the level of a Pratyekabuddha, while only one or two have been established on the stage of non-retrogression."
or they remain [in that state]. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is difficult to realize for those who are indolent, of inferior vigor, of inferior resolve, and lacking in wisdom.

Here, Kauśika, with my unobstructed Buddha-eye, I see in the northeastern direction, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, immeasurable and incalculable beings practicing for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; yet,
being devoid of skill in means regarding the perfection of wisdom, only one or two among them are established on the stage of non-retrogression.
They mostly abide on the level of a śrāvaka or on the level of a pratyekabuddha. For what reason? Because, Kauśika, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is difficult to realize.

By those who are indolent, lacking in vigor, deficient in resolve, and of poor wisdom. Here, Kauśika, with my unobstructed Buddha-eye, I see in the eastern-southern direction, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, immeasurable and incalculable beings practicing for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

Devoid of the perfection of wisdom and skillful means, only one or two among them will be established on the stage of non-retrogression; for the most part, they remain on the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha. Why is that? Because, Kauśika, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is difficult to realize.

By those who are indolent, lacking in vigor, of inferior resolve, and of poor wisdom. Here, Kauśika, with my unobstructed Buddha-eye, I see in the southern-western direction, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, immeasurable and incalculable beings practicing for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

Devoid of the perfection of wisdom and skill in means, only one or two among them will be established on the stage of non-retrogression; for the most part, they remain on the stage of a śrāvaka or the stage of a pratyekabuddha. Why is that? Because, Kauśika, supreme perfect enlightenment is difficult to realize.

By those who are indolent, lacking in vigor, deficient in resolve, and of poor wisdom. Here, Kauśika, with my unobstructed Buddha-eye, I see in the northwestern direction, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, immeasurable and incalculable beings practicing for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

Those who are devoid of skill in means regarding the perfection of wisdom—only one or two among them will be established on the stage of non-retrogression; for the most part, they remain on the stage of a śrāvaka or the stage of a pratyekabuddha. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is indeed difficult to realize.

By those who are indolent, lacking in vigor, deficient in resolve, and of poor wisdom. Here, Kauśika, with my unobstructed Buddha-eye, I see in the world-systems of the lower direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, immeasurable and incalculable beings who, being devoid of the perfection of wisdom and skill in means for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, have only one or two of them established on the stage of non-retrogression, while the vast majority [are established] on the stage of the Śrāvakas or the stage of the Pratyekabuddhas.
Or they remain [in that state]. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is difficult to realize for those who are indolent, lacking in vigor, having inferior resolve, and lacking in wisdom.

Here, Kauśika, with my unobstructed Buddha-eye, I see in the worlds of the upper direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, immeasurable and incalculable beings who, being devoid of the skillful means of the perfection of wisdom, set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; yet from among them, only one or two become established on the stage of non-retrogression, while the vast majority remain on the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha. For what reason is that?

For, Kauśika, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is difficult to realize for those who are indolent, lacking in vigor, inferior in character, inferior in resolve, and lacking in wisdom. Therefore, Kauśika, as for those sons of good family and daughters of good family who [are intent] upon unsurpassed perfect enlightenment...

Those who have set out and desire to quickly and easily awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment must frequently hear, take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and attend to this perfection of wisdom in a proper manner.
Having taken up, borne in mind, recited, mastered, and attended to this perfection of wisdom in a proper manner, they [should proceed].
All the dharmas of all the Buddhas should be brought to mind.

They are as follows: the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom;
internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, and great emptiness.

emptiness of the ultimate truth, emptiness of the conditioned, emptiness of the unconditioned, absolute emptiness, emptiness of that which has no beginning or end, emptiness of non-dispersal, emptiness of intrinsic nature, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of specific characteristics, emptiness of non-apprehension, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of self-nature, and emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence.

The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the four noble truths,
the four meditative absorptions, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, and the nine successive meditative attainments.

The three gates of liberation, the five superknowledges, all meditative concentrations, all gateways of dhāraṇīs, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha— furthermore,

whatever other immeasurable qualities of a Buddha are included within this perfection of wisdom, those too should be taken up, retained, recited, mastered, and properly attended to with right reflection.
For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, those sons of good family and daughters of good family will understand thus:

"In this very place, the Tathāgata formerly trained in the conduct of a bodhisattva, namely, in the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, and the perfection of ethical discipline."
In internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness,

great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end, the emptiness of non-dispersal, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of all phenomena.
In the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of non-apprehension, the emptiness of non-existence,
the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;
in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, and the five faculties.

In the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the four noble truths, the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), the nine successive dwellings in attainment (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), the three gateways to liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), the five superknowledges (*abhijñā*), all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), all gateways of dhāraṇī (*dhāraṇīmukha*), and the ten...

In the powers of a Tathāgata, in the four grounds of self-confidence, in the four analytical knowledges, in great loving-kindness, in great compassion, in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or in other immeasurable qualities of a Buddha.
We too must train ourselves accordingly; this Perfection of Wisdom is our Teacher.

Indeed, all other immeasurable Buddha-qualities are the teaching of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as well as that of the Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, Anāgāmins, Sakṛdāgāmins, and Srotāpannas—namely, this Perfection of Wisdom. It is within this Perfection of Wisdom...

Training in the perfection of meditation, training in the perfection of vigor, training in the perfection of patience, training in the perfection of ethical discipline, training in the perfection of generosity,
and training in internal emptiness.
Training in external emptiness,
training in internal-external emptiness,
and training in the emptiness of emptiness;
Training in great emptiness,
training in ultimate emptiness,
and training in conditioned emptiness.
Training in the emptiness of the unconditioned,
training in the emptiness of the ultimate, and training in the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end.
Training in the emptiness of non-dispersal,
training in the emptiness of intrinsic nature,
and training in the emptiness of all phenomena.
Training in the emptiness of specific characteristics,
training in the emptiness of non-apprehension,
and training in the emptiness of non-existence.
Training in the emptiness of intrinsic nature,
training in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence,
and training in the applications of mindfulness.
Training in the right efforts,
training in the bases of psychic power,
and training in the faculties.
Training in the powers, training in the factors of enlightenment,
and training in the noble eightfold path.
Training in the noble truths,
training in the meditative absorptions,
and training in the immeasurables.
training in the formless attainments,
training in the liberations,
and training in the successive meditative attainments;
Training in the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
training in the superknowledges;
training in the meditative concentrations.
Training in the gateways of dhāraṇīs,
training in the powers of a Tathāgata,
and training in the grounds of self-confidence.
Training in the analytical knowledges,
training in great loving-kindness,
and training in great compassion.
Training in the unique qualities of a Buddha,
training in omniscience, and training in the knowledge of the aspects of the path.
Training in this, training in omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*),

the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, Non-returners (*anāgāmin*), Once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*), and Stream-enterers (*srotaāpanna*) have gone, are going, and will go to the further shore.
Therefore, Kausika, whether the Tathagata is present or has passed into parinirvana, sons of good family or daughters of good family should honor the perfection of wisdom alone. For what reason?

Kauśika, this very perfection of wisdom is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed the refuge for all beings, including gods, humans, and asuras; likewise, the perfection of meditation itself must be honored by them. Why is that?

Kauśika, it is because this very perfection of meditation is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed the refuge for all beings, including gods, humans, and asuras.
They should instead honor the perfection of vigor itself. Why is that?
Because, Kauśika, this very perfection of vigor is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed the refuge for all beings, including gods, humans, and asuras.
They should instead honor the perfection of patience itself. Why is that?

Kauśika, this very perfection of patience is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed the refuge for all beings including gods, humans, and asuras; it is precisely this perfection of ethical discipline that they should honor. Why is that?

Kauśika, this very perfection of ethical discipline is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed the refuge for all beings including gods, humans, and asuras.
They should instead honor the perfection of giving itself. Why is that?
Kauśika, this very perfection of giving is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and it is the refuge for all beings, including gods, humans, and asuras.
They should instead honor internal emptiness itself. Why is that?

Kauśika, this very perfection of wisdom is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, as well as for the entire world with its gods, humans, and asuras; indeed, external emptiness itself is what they must revere. Why is that?
Kauśika, it is because this very external emptiness [is the basis] for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas.

It is the refuge, even unto the entire realm of beings including gods, humans, and asuras. That very emptiness of the internal and external (adhyātmabahirdhāśūnyatā) is what they should honor. Why is that?

Because, Kauśika, this very emptiness of the internal and external is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, even unto the entire realm of beings including gods, humans, and asuras.
They must repay that kindness by means of emptiness itself. For what reason?
Kauśika, this very emptiness of emptiness is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed for all beings, including gods, humans, and asuras.
They should honor great emptiness itself. Why is that?
Kauśika, this very great emptiness is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed the refuge for all beings, including gods, humans, and asuras;
they should honor ultimate emptiness itself. Why is that?

Kauśika, this very emptiness of the ultimate truth is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed for the entire world of beings, including gods, humans, and asuras;
it is precisely this emptiness of the conditioned that they must honor. Why is that?

Kauśika, it is because this very emptiness of the conditioned is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed for the entire world of beings, including gods, humans, and asuras.
They should honor unconditioned emptiness itself. Why is that?
Kauśika, this very unconditioned emptiness is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, and indeed for all beings including gods, humans, and asuras;
they should honor absolute emptiness itself. Why is that?

This very absolute emptiness, Kauśika, is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed for all beings including gods, humans, and asuras; it is this very emptiness without beginning or end that they must revere. Why is that?

Because this very emptiness without beginning or end, Kauśika, is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed for all beings including gods, humans, and asuras.
They should honor non-dispersal emptiness (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*) alone. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, this very non-dispersal emptiness is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed for all beings including gods, humans, and asuras;
they should honor natural emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) alone. For what reason?
Kauśika, this very emptiness of intrinsic nature is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed for all beings including gods, humans, and asuras;
by them, the emptiness of all dharmas alone must be honored. Why is that?
Kauśika, it is because this very emptiness of all dharmas is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed for all beings including gods, humans, and asuras.
They must honor precisely this emptiness of specific characteristics. For what reason?
Kauśika, this very emptiness of specific characteristics is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and indeed for all beings including gods, humans, and asuras;
it is precisely the emptiness of non-apprehension.
They should be honored by them. Why is that?

Kauśika, this very non-apprehension-emptiness is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed for all beings including gods, humans, and asuras; it is precisely this emptiness of non-existence that they should honor. Why is that?

This very emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), Kauśika, is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed the refuge for all beings including gods, humans, and asuras;
it is this very emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) that they must honor. Why is that?

Because this very emptiness of intrinsic nature, Kauśika, is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed the refuge for all beings including gods, humans, and asuras.
They must revere emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence itself. Why is that?

Because, Kauśika, this very emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed for all beings including gods, humans, and asuras. They must revere the foundations of mindfulness themselves. Why is that?

Kauśika, these very foundations of mindfulness are the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed for all beings including gods, humans, and asuras; likewise, the right efforts themselves are to be honored by them. Why is that?
Kauśika, these very right efforts are the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed for all beings including gods, humans, and asuras.
They should honor the bases of psychic power themselves. Why is that?
Kauśika, these very bases of psychic power are the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed the refuge for all beings, including gods, humans, and asuras.
They should honor the faculties themselves. Why is that?

Kauśika, these very faculties are the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed the refuge for all beings, including gods, humans, and asuras; they must honor these very powers. Why is that?
Kauśika, these very powers are the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed the refuge for all beings, including gods, humans, and asuras.
They should indeed revere the factors of enlightenment themselves. For what reason?

Because, Kauśika, these very factors of enlightenment are the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, and even for the entire world including its gods, humans, and asuras.
They should likewise revere the noble eightfold path itself. For what reason?

Kauśika, this very Noble Eightfold Path is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed the refuge for all beings, including gods, humans, and asuras; it is the Noble Truths themselves that they must revere. Why is that?
Kauśika, these very Noble Truths are the refuge for all Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, and indeed the refuge for all beings including gods, humans, and asuras;
the meditative absorptions (dhyānas) alone are to be honored by them. Why is that?
Kauśika, these very meditative absorptions are the refuge for all Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, and indeed the refuge for all beings including gods, humans, and asuras.
They themselves must revere the immeasurables. Why is that?

Because, Kauśika, these very immeasurables are the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, and indeed the refuge for all beings, including gods, humans, and asuras; they themselves must revere the formless attainments. Why is that?

Kauśika, these very formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) are the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed for all beings including gods, humans, and asuras; they alone are to be honored by them as liberations. Why is that?
Kauśika, these very liberations (*vimokṣa*) are the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and they are the refuge for all beings including gods, humans, and asuras.
They should honor only the successive attainments of the meditative states. Why is that?

Kauśika, these very successive attainments of the meditative states are the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed the refuge for the entire world of beings, including its gods, humans, and asuras.
They should honor precisely these gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Why is that?

Kauśika, these very gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are the refuge for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as for bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas, and indeed the refuge for the entire world of beings, including gods, humans, and asuras.
They themselves must revere the superknowledges (abhijñā). For what reason?

Kauśika, these very superknowledges are the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and even the refuge for the entire world including its gods, humans, and asuras; they themselves must revere the meditative concentrations (samādhi) as well. For what reason?

Kauśika, these very concentrations are the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed the refuge for all beings, including gods, humans, and asuras; they must honor these very gateways of dhāraṇī. Why is that?

Because, Kauśika, these very gateways of dhāraṇī are the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed the refuge for all beings, including gods, humans, and asuras.
They should instead honor the powers of the Tathāgata themselves. Why is that?
Kauśika, these very powers of the Tathāgata are the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed the refuge for all beings, including gods, humans, and asuras.
They should honor these very grounds of self-confidence. Why is that?

Because, Kauśika, these very grounds of self-confidence are the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed for all beings including gods, humans, and asuras; they should honor these very analytical knowledges. Why is that?
Kauśika, these very analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and even for the world with its gods, humans, and asuras;
yet it is great compassion alone that they must revere in return. Why is that?
Because, Kauśika, this very great compassion is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and it is the refuge for the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
Only the unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇikabuddhadharma) should be honored by them. Why is that?
Kauśika, these very unique qualities of a Buddha are the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed for all beings including gods, humans, and asuras;
rather, it is omniscience itself that should be honored by them. Why is that?

Kauśika, these very [knowledges]—namely, the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*)—are the refuge for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as for the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, and indeed for the entire world with its gods, humans, and asuras; they alone are to be honored by them. Why is that?

Because, Kauśika, these very knowledges of the aspects of the path are the refuge for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as for the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, and indeed for the entire world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
They should instead honor omniscience itself. Why is that?
Kauśika, it is this very omniscience that is the refuge for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and indeed for all beings, including gods, humans, and asuras.

For if, Kauśika, some son of good family or daughter of good family, after the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa, should have a stūpa made of the seven precious gems for the sake of worship— one yojana in height and half a yojana in width and length— and should, for as long as they live, honor it with divine flowers, divine garlands, divine perfumes, divine ointments, divine powders, and divine robes;

One should honor, revere, respect, and worship [the Bodhisattva] with divine parasols, divine banners, divine flags, and divine musical instruments. What do you think, Kauśika? Would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
Śakra said: “Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
The Blessed One said:
“Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family [obtains] a much greater [merit].”

One who writes down this perfection of wisdom, and having written it, takes it up, bears it in mind, recites it, masters it, attends to it thoroughly, and does not depart from the mind of omniscience for others, and furthermore honors, reveres, respects, and worships it with flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, and parasols— such a person generates merit.
With banners, flags, and various musical instruments—
let there stand, Kauśika, even a single stūpa. For if, Kauśika, some son of good family or daughter of good family, after the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa,
were to fill this Jambudvīpa with stūpas made of the seven precious gems, each one yojana in height and half a yojana in width.
And suppose one were to honor, revere, respect, and worship them for as long as life lasts with divine flowers,
divine garlands, divine perfumes, divine ointments, divine powders, divine robes,
divine garments, divine parasols, divine banners, divine flags, and divine musical instruments. What do you think?
"Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
The Blessed One said:

Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family produces much greater merit who, having written down this perfection of wisdom, shall take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, and attend to it with proper mental attention,
and who shall not be separated from the mind of omniscience.
And furthermore, Kauśika, he will honor, revere, respect, and worship it with flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags,
and various kinds of musical instruments—
even if this Jambudvīpa were filled to the brim with stūpas of the Tathāgata.

If, Kauśika, a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to fill this world-system of four great continents with stūpas made of the seven precious gems— stūpas one yojana high and half a yojana wide— and were to honor, revere, respect, and worship them throughout their entire life with divine flowers and divine [incense], etc.
With divine garlands, divine perfumes, divine ointments, divine powders, divine robes,

divine garments, divine parasols, divine banners, divine flags, and divine musical instruments— what do you think, Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family will generate even more merit than that."
Whoever shall take up this Perfection of Wisdom, having made it into a book, shall preserve it, recite it, master it, and attend to it with wise reflection;

and having written it down, shall honor it, revere it, esteem it, and worship it with flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, flags, and various kinds of musical instruments.
"Let alone, Kauśika, a world-system of four great continents filled with stūpas of the Tathāgata. If, Kauśika,

a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to fill this trichiliocosm, after the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa, for the purpose of worship with stūpas made of the seven precious gems, each one yojana in height and half a yojana in width..."
And suppose one were to honor, revere, respect, and worship them for as long as life lasts with divine flowers,
divine garlands, divine fragrances, divine ointments, divine powders, divine robes,
divine garments, divine parasols, divine banners, divine flags, and divine musical instruments. What do you think?
"Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
The Blessed One said:

Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family will generate much greater merit who, having made this Perfection of Wisdom into a book, shall take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, and attend to it with wise reflection; and who shall honor it, revere it, esteem it, and worship it.

With flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and various kinds of musical instruments— let alone, Kauśika, a thousandfold world-system filled with stūpas of the Tathāgata; if, Kauśika,
a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to [fill] this middle three-thousandfold world-system with stūpas of the Tathāgata after he has passed into parinirvāṇa...

For the sake of worship, one might fill [the world] with stupas made of the seven precious gems, one yojana high and half a yojana wide, and honor, revere, respect, and worship them until the end of time with divine flowers,
divine garlands, divine perfumes, divine ointments, divine powders, and divine robes.

With divine garments, divine parasols, divine banners, divine flags, and divine musical instruments—what do you think, Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account? Śakra said: Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.

The Blessed One said: "Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family will generate much greater merit who, having written down this Perfection of Wisdom, shall take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, and attend to it with wise reflection."
He will honor, revere, respect, and worship [them] with flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and various kinds of musical instruments.

Let alone, Kauśika, a second-order intermediate world-system filled with stūpas of the Tathāgata; if, Kauśika, a son of good family or a daughter of good family, after the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa...

For the sake of worship, one might fill this great trichiliocosm with stūpas for the Tathāgata made of the seven precious gems after the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa— stūpas one yojana in height and half a yojana in width— and honor them, revere them, respect them, and worship them with divine flowers, divine garlands, divine perfumes, and divine [incenses].
With divine ointments, divine powders, divine robes, divine parasols, divine banners, divine flags,
and divine musical instruments— what do you think, Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One! Much, Sugata!
The Blessed One said:

Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family will generate far more merit who, having written down this perfection of wisdom, shall take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, attend to it with wise reflection, and honor, revere, respect, and worship it.

With flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and various musical instruments— let it be so, Kauśika, even if this great trichiliocosm world-system were filled with stūpas of the Tathāgata; and whatever beings there may be, Kauśika, in this great trichiliocosm world-system, let each single being, after the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa...
For the sake of worship, one should have a stūpa made of the seven precious gems constructed; and for as long as life lasts, one should honor, revere, respect,
and worship it with divine flowers, divine garlands, divine perfumes, divine ointments, divine powders, divine robes, divine parasols, divine banners, divine flags, and divine musical instruments.

And whichever son of good family or daughter of good family, having written down this perfection of wisdom, shall take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, and attend to it with proper mental attention,
and who shall not be separated from the mind of omniscience,
and who shall honor, revere, respect, and worship it—
With flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and various kinds of musical instruments, this person would generate much more merit than that.

Śakra said: "So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata. By those who honor, revere, respect, and worship the perfection of wisdom, Blessed One, they honor, revere, respect, and worship the Tathāgatas, Arhats [of the] past, future, and present."
They would honor, revere, esteem, and worship the perfectly enlightened Buddhas;

and suppose that as many beings as there are in world-systems in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, each single being, after the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa, were to construct for the sake of worship a stūpa made of the seven precious gems, one *yojana* in height.
If one were to honor, revere, respect, and worship them for an eon or the remainder of an eon with an extent of one yojana,
using divine flowers, divine garlands, divine perfumes, divine ointments, divine powders, divine robes, divine parasols, divine banners, divine flags, and divine musical instruments;
Suppose there were as many sentient beings in as many world systems in the southern direction as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges; and suppose that each single sentient being,

after the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa, were to construct for the sake of worship a stūpa made of the seven precious gems, one yojana in height and one yojana in width, and were to honor, revere, respect, and worship them for an eon or for the remainder of an eon.
With divine flowers, divine garlands, divine perfumes, divine ointments, divine powders, divine robes, divine parasols, divine banners, divine flags, and divine musical instruments—
just as many beings as there are in world-systems in the western direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, from each and every one of those beings...

After the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa, for the sake of worship, one might cause a stūpa made of the seven precious gems to be built— one yojana in height and one yojana in width— and for an eon or the remainder of an eon, one might honor, revere, respect, and worship it with divine flowers, divine garlands, divine perfumes, divine ointments, and divine powders.
With divine robes, divine parasols, divine banners, divine flags, and divine musical instruments—

suppose that as many beings as there are in world systems in the northern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, were each to construct a stūpa made of the seven precious gems, one yojana in height, for the sake of honoring the Tathāgata after his parinirvāṇa.

And suppose one were to honor, revere, respect, and worship them for an eon or the remainder of an eon, with a width of one yojana, using divine flowers, divine garlands, divine perfumes, divine ointments, divine powders, divine robes, divine parasols, divine banners, divine flags, and divine musical instruments.
Suppose that as many beings as there are in world-systems in the northeastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, and each single being,

after the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa, were to construct for the sake of worship a stūpa made of the seven precious jewels— one *yojana* in height and half a *yojana* in width— and were to honor, revere, and respect them for an eon or for the remainder of an eon.
One should worship with divine flowers, divine garlands, divine scents, divine ointments, divine powders, divine robes, divine parasols, divine banners, divine flags, and divine musical instruments—
as many as there are beings in as many world-systems in the southeastern direction as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, with each single being [worshipping].

Suppose a being, after the Tathāgata has entered final nirvāṇa, were to cause a stūpa made of the seven precious gems to be built— one yojana in height and one yojana in width— and were to honor, revere, respect, and worship it for an eon or the remainder of an eon with divine flowers, divine garlands, divine perfumes, divine ointments, and divine [incenses].
With divine powders, divine robes, divine parasols, divine banners, divine flags, and divine musical instruments—

suppose that as many beings as there are in world systems in the southwestern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, were each to construct a stūpa made of the seven precious gems, one *yojana* in height, for the sake of honoring the Tathāgata after his final nirvāṇa.
If one were to honor, revere, respect, and worship them for an eon or the remainder of an eon with a distance of a yojana, using divine flowers, divine garlands, divine perfumes, divine ointments,
divine powders, divine robes, divine parasols, divine banners, divine flags, and divine musical instruments;

Suppose there were as many sentient beings in as many world-systems in the northwestern direction as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges; and suppose that each single sentient being, after the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa, were to construct for the sake of worship a stūpa made of the seven precious gems, one yojana in height and one yojana in width, and were to honor, revere, and respect it for an eon or for the remainder of an eon.

One should worship with divine flowers, divine garlands, divine perfumes, divine ointments, divine powders, divine robes, divine parasols, divine banners, divine flags, and divine musical instruments—
as many beings as there are in the world systems below, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, so that each single being [worships].

After the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa, for the sake of worship, one might cause a stūpa made of the seven precious jewels to be built— one yojana in height and one yojana in width— and for an eon or the remainder of an eon, one might honor, revere, respect, and worship it with divine flowers, divine garlands, divine perfumes, divine ointments, and divine powders.
With divine robes, divine parasols, divine banners, divine flags, and divine musical instruments—

suppose that as many beings as there are in the world systems in the direction above, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, were each to construct a stūpa made of the seven precious gems, one *yojana* in height, for the sake of honoring the Tathāgata after his final nirvāṇa.
And for an extent of one yojana, one might honor, revere, respect, and worship them for an eon or the remainder of an eon with divine flowers, divine garlands, divine perfumes,
divine ointments, divine powders, divine robes, divine parasols, divine banners, and divine flags.
and with musical instruments. What do you think, Blessed One? Would that son of good family or daughter of good family, Kauśika, generate much merit on that account?
The Blessed One said:
"Much, Kauśika.

Śakra said: "Therefore, Blessed One, that son of good family or daughter of good family produces much more merit who, having written down this Perfection of Wisdom, shall take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, and master it."
And he will attend to them with wise attention, and he will honor, revere, respect,
and worship them with flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and various kinds of musical instruments. That...

For what reason? Because, Blessed One, all wholesome dharmas are included within this perfection of wisdom; that is to say: the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the six perfections—namely, the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom.

Internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end,
the emptiness of non-dispersal, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of specific characteristics, and the emptiness of non-apprehension.
The emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

The foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the three gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—the four noble truths: suffering and the origin of suffering...

The path leading to the cessation of suffering; the six supernormal knowledges; the eight liberations; the nine successive meditative attainments; all concentrations; all doors of dhāraṇī; the ten powers of a Tathāgata; the four grounds of self-confidence; the four analytical knowledges; great loving-kindness; great compassion; the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; omniscience; the knowledge of the aspects of the path; and the knowledge of all aspects.

This is that teaching of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, wherein all the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— past, future, and present— having trained, have gone and will go to the further shore of all dharmas.
This is the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Hundred Thousand," of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Then the Blessed One said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"So it is, Kauśika, so it is."

Those sons of good family or daughters of good family will produce much merit— immeasurable, incalculable, inconceivable, incomparable, and limitless— those sons of good family or daughters of good family who, having written down this perfection of wisdom and made it into a book, will take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, and master it.
And they will attend to it with wise attention,
and furthermore, they will honor,
revere, respect, and worship it with flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and various kinds of musical instruments. Why is that?

For it is from the perfection of wisdom, Kauśika, that the omniscience of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas is derived; the perfection of meditation is derived from the perfection of wisdom; the perfection of vigor is derived from the perfection of wisdom;

the perfection of patience is derived from the perfection of wisdom; the perfection of ethical discipline is derived from the perfection of wisdom; and the perfection of generosity is derived from the perfection of wisdom.
They have issued forth from the perfection of wisdom.
Internal emptiness has issued forth from the perfection of wisdom;
external emptiness has issued forth from the perfection of wisdom.
Internal-and-external emptiness is produced from the perfection of wisdom;
the emptiness of emptiness is produced from the perfection of wisdom;
great emptiness is produced from the perfection of wisdom.
Ultimate emptiness is brought forth by the perfection of wisdom; conditioned emptiness is brought forth by the perfection of wisdom;
unconditioned emptiness is brought forth by the perfection of wisdom.
The emptiness of the ultimate is produced from the perfection of wisdom; the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end is produced from the perfection of wisdom;
the emptiness of non-dispersal is produced from the perfection of wisdom.
The emptiness of intrinsic nature is brought forth by the perfection of wisdom; the emptiness of all phenomena is brought forth by the perfection of wisdom;
the emptiness of specific characteristics is brought forth by the perfection of wisdom.
The emptiness of non-apprehension is brought forth by the perfection of wisdom; the emptiness of non-existence is brought forth by the perfection of wisdom;
the emptiness of intrinsic nature is brought forth by the perfection of wisdom.
The emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is produced from the perfection of wisdom;
the applications of mindfulness are produced from the perfection of wisdom;
the right efforts are produced from the perfection of wisdom.
The bases of psychic power are produced from the perfection of wisdom; the faculties are produced from the perfection of wisdom;
the powers are produced from the perfection of wisdom.
The factors of enlightenment are produced from the perfection of wisdom;
the noble eightfold path is produced from the perfection of wisdom;
the noble truths are produced from the perfection of wisdom.
The meditative absorptions are produced from the perfection of wisdom; the immeasurables are produced from the perfection of wisdom;
the formless attainments are produced from the perfection of wisdom.
The eight liberations are brought forth by the perfection of wisdom;
the nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling are brought forth by the perfection of wisdom;
and the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are brought forth by the perfection of wisdom.
The superknowledges are produced from the perfection of wisdom;
the meditative concentrations are produced from the perfection of wisdom;
the gateways of mnemonic formulas are produced from the perfection of wisdom.
The ten powers of a Tathāgata are brought forth from the perfection of wisdom; the four grounds of self-confidence are brought forth from the perfection of wisdom;
the analytical knowledges are brought forth from the perfection of wisdom.
Great loving-kindness is brought forth from the perfection of wisdom; great compassion is brought forth from the perfection of wisdom;
the unique qualities of a buddha are brought forth from the perfection of wisdom.
The five eyes of the Tathāgata are produced from the perfection of wisdom;
the maturation of sentient beings and the purification of the Buddha-field are produced from the perfection of wisdom;
for indeed, Kauśika, omniscience itself is produced from the perfection of wisdom.
The knowledge of the aspects of the path is produced from the perfection of wisdom; the knowledge of all aspects is produced from the perfection of wisdom;
for indeed, Kauśika, the vehicle of the śrāvakas is produced from the perfection of wisdom.
For indeed, Kauśika, the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas issues forth from the perfection of wisdom; for indeed, Kauśika, the Mahāyāna issues forth from the perfection of wisdom;
for indeed, Kauśika, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment [issues forth from it].

Therefore, Kauśika, if any son of good family or daughter of good family, having written down this perfection of wisdom and made it into a book, shall take it up, bear it in mind, master it, and attend to it properly, and shall honor, revere, respect, and worship it;

Kauśika, compared to this accumulation of merit consisting of flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and various kinds of musical instruments, that former accumulation of merit does not approach even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part.
It does not even admit of a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousand-millionth part, nor any number, nor a fraction, nor a calculation, nor a comparison, nor even a resemblance. Why is that?
Because, Kauśika, as long as this perfection of wisdom remains in Jambudvīpa, for that long the Jewel of the Buddha will not disappear.
There will be no disappearance of the Jewel of the Dharma; there will be no disappearance of the Jewel of the Saṅgha.
For that long, the ten paths of wholesome action will appear in the world; the four dhyānas will appear in the world;
and the four immeasurables will appear in the world.
There will be the manifestation in the world of the four formless attainments;
there will be the manifestation of the five superknowledges.
There will be the manifestation in the world of the perfection of generosity.
The perfection of ethical discipline will appear in the world; the perfection of patience will appear in the world;
the perfection of vigor will appear in the world.
The perfection of meditation will appear in the world; the perfection of wisdom will appear in the world.
The emptiness of the internal will appear in the world.
The appearance of external emptiness will occur in the world;
the appearance of internal-external emptiness will occur in the world;
the appearance of the emptiness of emptiness will occur in the world.
The great emptiness will appear in the world;
the ultimate emptiness will appear in the world.
The appearance of the emptiness of the conditioned will occur in the world;
the appearance of the emptiness of the unconditioned will occur in the world;
the appearance of absolute emptiness will occur in the world.
The emptiness of that which has no beginning or end will appear in the world;
the emptiness of non-dispersal will appear in the world; the emptiness of intrinsic nature will appear in the world.
The emptiness of all phenomena will appear in the world;
the emptiness of specific characteristics will appear in the world;
the emptiness of non-apprehension will appear in the world.
The manifestation of the emptiness of non-existence will occur in the world;
the manifestation of the emptiness of intrinsic nature will occur in the world;
the manifestation of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence will occur in the world.
The appearance of the foundations of mindfulness will occur in the world;
the appearance of the right efforts will occur in the world;
the appearance of the bases of psychic power will occur in the world.
The appearance of the sense-faculties will occur in the world;
