In that case, Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom should be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, with flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes,
umbrellas, banners, flags, and various kinds of musical instruments. And having written it down, it should be honored, revered, and esteemed.
They should be honored with flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and various kinds of musical instruments.
For whoever, O Blessed One, shall take up this perfection of wisdom, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, and attend to it with wise reflection—
And having written it down, he will honor, revere, respect,
and worship it with flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and various kinds of musical instruments.
For such a person, rebirth in the hells should not be expected, nor rebirth in the animal realm, nor rebirth in the world of Yama;

neither the level of a Śrāvaka nor the level of a Pratyekabuddha should be expected, until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. And they shall never be separated from the vision of the Tathāgata and from the ripening of sentient beings as they travel from buddha-field to buddha-field.
And one should honor, revere, respect, and worship those Tathāgatas, Arhats,

and Perfectly Enlightened Ones with flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and various kinds of musical instruments. Furthermore, Blessed One, suppose this triple-thousandfold world system were filled to the very top with the relics of the Tathāgatas.
Since this perfection of wisdom is written out and offered, O Blessed One, of these two portions, I would take this very perfection of wisdom. Why is that?
Because, O Blessed One, it is from this that the Tathāgatas have emerged, and those relics of the Tathāgatas are derived from it; therefore, they are the relics of the Tathāgatas.

Those sons of good family and daughters of good family who honor, revere, respect, and worship these [teachings] do not go to an evil destiny or a state of ruin. Having experienced divine and human prosperities,
they attain final nirvana according to their aspiration— whether by means of the vehicle of the disciples or the vehicle of the solitary buddhas.
Or even by means of the vehicle of the perfectly enlightened ones;
moreover, Blessed One, the vision of the Tathāgata and the vision of the perfection of wisdom—these two are equal. For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom and the Tathāgata are non-dual and not divided into two.

Furthermore, Blessed One, whatever Dharma a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha might teach while abiding in the three miracles—namely, the discourses (sūtra), mixed prose and verse (geya), prophecies (vyākaraṇa), verses (gāthā), inspired utterances (udāna), introductory narratives (nidāna), legends (ityuktaka), birth stories (jātaka), extensive teachings (vaipulya), marvelous events (adbhutadharma), parables (avadāna), and instructions (upadeśa)—and whatever a son of good family or daughter of good family, having taken up and mastered this Perfection of Wisdom, might teach to another: these two are equal. Why is that?
For, Blessed One, it is from this that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have emerged; thus have the three miracles emerged.
It is from this that the Sūtras, Geyas, Vyākaraṇas, Gāthās, Udānas, Nidānas, Ityuktakas, Jātakas, Vaipulyas, Adbhutadharmas, Avadānas, and Upadeśas have emerged.
Furthermore, Blessed One, as for those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in the eastern direction, who are as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā—

In the southern direction, there are Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas; in the western direction, there are Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas; in the northern direction, there are Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas.
In the northeastern direction, there are Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas; in the southeastern direction, there are Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas;
in the southwestern direction... [ŚsP_II-4_105]

In that direction are Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas; in the northwestern direction are Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas; in the downward direction are Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas.
In the direction above, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas,

abiding in the three miraculous displays, teach the Dharma: the discourses (sūtra), mixed prose and verse (geya), prophecies (vyākaraṇa), verses (gāthā), inspired utterances (udāna), introductory narratives (nidāna), parables (ityuktaka), birth stories (jātaka), extensive teachings (vaipulya), marvelous accounts (adbhutadharma), and instructions (avadānopadeśa).
And if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having taken up and mastered this perfection of wisdom, were to teach it to another, these two are equal. Why is that?
For it is from this [perfection of wisdom] that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in the ten directions have emerged; it is from this that they have emerged.

The three miracles; the discourses (sūtra), mixed prose and verse (geya), prophecies (vyākaraṇa), verses (gāthā), inspired utterances (udāna), introductory narratives (nidāna), parables (ityuktaka), birth stories (jātaka), extensive teachings (vaipulya), marvelous events (adbhutadharma), legends (avadāna), and instructions (upadeśa) have emerged from this.

Furthermore, Blessed One, if those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones in each of the ten directions—in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges—were to be honored, revered, and respected...

They should worship it with flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and various kinds of musical instruments. And whoever, having written out the book of the *prajñāpāramitā*,
should honor it, revere it, esteem it, and worship it with flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, and robes...
This is equal to [honoring them] with parasols, banners, flags, and various musical instruments. For what reason?
Because from this [perfection of wisdom] have the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas emerged.
Furthermore, Blessed One, a son of good family or a daughter of good family will take up this Prajñāpāramitā.

Whoever shall uphold, recite, master, and attend to it with wise reflection, and shall reveal it in detail to others—for such a person, rebirth in the hells is not to be expected; nor is rebirth in the animal realm or the world of Yama to be expected;
nor is the level of a Śrāvaka or the level of a Pratyekabuddha to be expected. Why is that?
For it should be known that such a son of good family or daughter of good family stands upon the stage of non-retrogression. Why is that?

Because, having written down this perfection of wisdom, they take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, and attend to it with wise reflection; and having written it down, they honor, revere, respect, and worship it with flowers.
With garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags,
and various musical instruments— for indeed, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom pacifies all fears and eradicates all diseases.
Furthermore, Blessed One, whichever son of good family or daughter of good family shall write down and take up this perfection of wisdom...
Whoever shall uphold, recite, master, and honor, revere, esteem,

and worship it with flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and various kinds of musical instruments— for such a person, no fear from any quarter is to be expected.
It is just as if,

Blessed One, a man terrified by the fear of a creditor were to serve a king and attend upon him; while serving and attending upon the king, he would serve him in such a way that he does not [fear] the very person from whom his fear originally arose.
He fears them. Why is that?
For it is thus, Blessed One, with one who relies upon a king or relies upon a powerful person.

In the same way, Blessed One, the relics of the Tathāgata receive worship because they have been permeated by the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Even that knowledge of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatājñāna*), Blessed One, is permeated by the perfection of wisdom.
Therefore, Blessed One, of these two limbs, I would choose this very perfection of wisdom. Why is that?
For, Blessed One, it is from this that the relics of the Tathāgata have emerged; it is from this that the thirty-two marks of a great man have emerged;
and it is from this that the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, and the four analytical knowledges of the Tathāgata have emerged.
The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇikabuddhadharma) have emerged from this;

great loving-kindness (mahāmaitrī) and great compassion (mahākaruṇā) have emerged from this. Blessed One, the five perfections (pāramitā) receive the designation "perfection" because they have emerged from this, up to and including the Tathāgata’s omniscience (sarvākārajñatā), which, Blessed One, [is present] in villages, towns, market towns, districts, kingdoms, and royal capitals.

And in whatever part of this trichiliocosm great trichiliocosm world-system this Perfection of Wisdom shall be taken up, maintained, recited, mastered, and having been written down, honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped— there,

no human or non-human being seeking an opportunity for entry or searching for an opening shall find such an opportunity. Furthermore, they shall all, in due course, become those whose nature is to attain final nirvana.
"Among the three vehicles, there is no preference for one vehicle over another. Thus, Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is of great benefit;

for indeed, Blessed One, in this triple-thousand great thousandfold world system, the appearance of a Buddha is to be expected among sentient beings by virtue of the truth of the Buddhas—namely, in whichever world system this perfection of wisdom shall circulate."
It is just as if, Blessed One, there were this priceless great jewel, and that great jewel were endowed with such qualities as these,
wherever that great jewel might be placed.
In whatever place non-human beings might find no opportunity for entry— whether it be a woman or a man possessed by a non-human being—
one should insert that great jewel there.
Then that non-human being, unable to endure the brilliance of that great jewel, would quickly depart and not remain;

or, if that great jewel were placed upon the body of one burning with bile, it would overcome that bile; or, if that great jewel were placed upon a body overwhelmed by phlegm, it would likewise overcome that [phlegm].

If that great maṇi-jewel were placed upon a body stiffened by phlegm, it would pacify even that phlegm; or if there were a disease arising from a disorder of the humors (*sāṃnipātika*), and that great maṇi-jewel were placed upon the body, it would pacify even that disorder of the humors so that it would not increase.
Furthermore, it would emit light at night, and when the hot season is present, in whatever place that great maṇi-jewel [is located]...
If it were placed there, it would make that region cool; and when the cold season is present, if that great maṇi-jewel were placed in whatever region, it would not make that region hot;
and on whichever spot of earth that great maṇi-jewel were placed, that spot of earth would not become excessively hot.
One should place that great maṇi-jewel on a spot of earth that is neither too cold nor too soft; one should not allow venomous serpents to frequent that spot of earth.
Furthermore, other creatures such as scorpions and reptiles would not frequent it. Blessed One, if any woman or man should be bitten by a venomous serpent, [they would be healed].
If one were to show that great maṇi-jewel to him, by the mere sight of it, that poison would vanish. Blessed One, that great maṇi-jewel would be endowed with such qualities as these:
Blessed One, for those women or men who have an *arbuda*, a *timira*, an *ajaka*, or any eye disease...
Whether it be a disease of the ear, a disease of the nose, a disease of the tongue, a disease of the throat, or a disease of the body— if that great maṇi-jewel were placed upon their bodies,

then their tumor, or their cataract, or their ajaka, or their eye disease, or their ear disease, or their nose disease, or their tongue disease, or their throat disease, or their body disease would be pacified.
O Blessed One, that great maṇi-jewel would be endowed with such qualities as these:
even if one were to cast that great maṇi-jewel into water, O Blessed One, that very water would become possessed of the eight qualities and become of a single color.

Blessed One, if that great maṇi-jewel were tied with a blue cloth and cast into water, the water would become blue by its very nature; if it were tied with a yellow cloth and cast into water, [the water would become yellow].
That water would indeed take on that very nature;
if that great jewel were bound with a red garment and cast into the water,
that water would indeed take on that very nature.
If that great maṇi-jewel were tied with a white robe and cast into water, that water would become white by its very nature;
if that great maṇi-jewel were tied with a madder-colored robe and cast into water, [the water would become red].
That water would indeed take on the nature of that [jewel];
if that great maṇi-jewel were tied with a crystal-colored robe and cast into the water, that water would indeed take on the nature of that [robe].
If one were to tie this great maṇi-jewel with these various kinds of robes and cast it into water, that water would become of its very same nature;
moreover, O Blessed One, whatever turbidity there might be in that water, that great maṇi-jewel would clarify it.
O Blessed One, it is endowed with such qualities as these.
That would be a great maṇi-jewel;
and likewise, Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is like a divine maṇi-jewel, being the source of all virtues and the liberator from all evils.
Then the venerable Ānanda said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"What do you think, Kauśika? Is this a divine jewel, or rather, is there such a jewel among the humans of Jambudvīpa?"
Śakra said: "Venerable sir, this is a divine jewel.

However, Venerable Ānanda, those great jewels belonging to the humans of Jambudvīpa are small and heavy, whereas those that are divine are large and light; in these respects, the [divine jewels] are far more perfectly complete than those of the humans of Jambudvīpa."

Just as the divine jewel-gems of humans do not approach even a fraction, a part, a calculation, a comparison, or a likeness of those Jambudvīpa gems, so too the latter do not approach the divine jewel-gems.
Then again, Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One:

Furthermore, Blessed One, whichever casket that great precious gem might be placed in, as soon as it has been placed there or even while it is being placed, that casket would become desirable because of those qualities of the precious gem; others too would conceive a longing for that casket.

In the same way, Blessed One, wherever this perfection of wisdom circulates, there those sons of good family or daughters of good family will have no physical or mental sufferings or calamities, whether caused by humans or non-humans.
"Great jewel," Blessed One, is a designation for the perfection of wisdom; it is a designation for the knowledge of all aspects.

"To what extent, Blessed One, can the qualities of the perfection of wisdom be proclaimed? For the qualities of the perfection of wisdom are indeed immeasurable; and those relics of the Tathāgata are due to the perfection of wisdom. To what extent, Blessed One, can the qualities of the perfection of meditation be proclaimed? For the qualities of the perfection of meditation are indeed immeasurable; and those relics of the Tathāgata are due to the perfection of meditation."

"O Blessed One, how much can be proclaimed of the qualities of the perfection of vigor? For the qualities of the perfection of vigor are indeed immeasurable; and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for that perfection of vigor.

O Blessed One, how much can be proclaimed of the qualities of the perfection of patience? For the qualities of the perfection of patience are indeed immeasurable; and those relics of the Tathāgata [are the vessel] for that perfection of patience.
O Blessed One, how much can be proclaimed of the qualities of the perfection of ethical discipline? For the qualities of the perfection of ethical discipline are indeed immeasurable."
The virtues of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) are the receptacle for those relics of the Tathāgata.

To what extent, Blessed One, is it possible to proclaim the virtues of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*)? For the virtues of the perfection of generosity are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the receptacle for the perfection of generosity. To what extent, Blessed One, is it possible to proclaim the virtues of internal emptiness (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*)? For the virtues of internal emptiness are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are [the receptacle] for internal emptiness.

“Blessed One, how many virtues of external emptiness can be proclaimed? For the virtues of external emptiness are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for that external emptiness.

Blessed One, how many virtues of internal-and-external emptiness can be proclaimed? For the virtues of internal-and-external emptiness are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for that internal-and-external emptiness.”

"To what extent, Blessed One, can the qualities of the emptiness of emptiness be proclaimed? For the qualities of the emptiness of emptiness are indeed immeasurable; and those relics of the Tathāgata are the very essence of the emptiness of emptiness.

To what extent, Blessed One, can the qualities of the great emptiness be proclaimed? For the qualities of the great emptiness are indeed immeasurable; and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for the great emptiness."

"To what extent, Blessed One, can the qualities of ultimate emptiness be proclaimed? For the qualities of ultimate emptiness are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are [the result] of ultimate emptiness. To what extent, Blessed One, can the qualities of conditioned emptiness be proclaimed? For the qualities of conditioned emptiness are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are [the result] of conditioned emptiness."

"Blessed One, how many qualities of the emptiness of the unconditioned can be proclaimed? For the qualities of the emptiness of the unconditioned are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are [the result] of that emptiness of the unconditioned.

Blessed One, how many qualities of the emptiness of the ultimate can be proclaimed? For the qualities of the emptiness of the ultimate are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are [the result] of that emptiness of the ultimate."

"To what extent, Blessed One, can the qualities of the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*) be proclaimed? For the qualities of the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are [the result] of that emptiness of that which is without beginning or end. To what extent, Blessed One, can the qualities of the emptiness of non-dispersal (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*) be proclaimed? For the qualities of the emptiness of non-dispersal are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are [the result] of that emptiness of non-dispersal."

"O Bhagavān, how many qualities of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛtiśūnyatā*) can be proclaimed? For the qualities of the emptiness of intrinsic nature are immeasurable; and those relics of the Tathāgata are [the result] of that emptiness of intrinsic nature.

O Bhagavān, how many qualities of the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaśūnyatā*) can be proclaimed? For the qualities of the emptiness of all phenomena are immeasurable; and those relics of the Tathāgata are [the result] of that emptiness of all phenomena. O Bhagavān, how many... [can be proclaimed]? (ŚsP_II-4_110)

The qualities of the emptiness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) are indeed immeasurable to proclaim; for the qualities of the emptiness of specific characteristics are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for that emptiness of specific characteristics.

"Blessed One, how many qualities of the emptiness of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*) can be proclaimed? For the qualities of the emptiness of non-apprehension are indeed immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for that emptiness of non-apprehension."

“Blessed One, how many qualities of the emptiness of non-existence can be proclaimed? For the qualities of the emptiness of non-existence are indeed immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for that emptiness of non-existence. Blessed One, how many qualities of the emptiness of intrinsic nature can be proclaimed? For the qualities of the emptiness of intrinsic nature are indeed immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are [the vessel] for that emptiness of intrinsic nature.”

"To what extent, Blessed One, can the qualities of the emptiness of the nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*) be proclaimed? For the qualities of the emptiness of the nature of non-existence are indeed immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for that emptiness of the nature of non-existence. To what extent, Blessed One, can the qualities of the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) be proclaimed? For the qualities of the applications of mindfulness are indeed immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for those applications of mindfulness."

“Blessed One, how much can be proclaimed of the qualities of the four right efforts? For the qualities of the right efforts are immeasurable; and those relics of the Tathāgata are the very vessels for those right efforts.

Blessed One, how much can be proclaimed of the qualities of the four bases of psychic power? For the qualities of the bases of psychic power are immeasurable; and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessels for those bases of psychic power.”

"How many, Blessed One, can the qualities of the five faculties be proclaimed? For the qualities of the faculties are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for those faculties.
How many, Blessed One, can the qualities of the five powers be proclaimed? For the qualities of the powers are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for those powers."

“Blessed One, how much can be proclaimed of the qualities of the seven factors of awakening? For the qualities of the factors of awakening are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for those factors of awakening.

Blessed One, how much can be proclaimed of the qualities of the noble eightfold path? For the qualities of the noble eightfold path are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for the noble eightfold path.”

“Blessed One, how much could one possibly proclaim of the qualities of the four noble truths? For the qualities of the noble truths are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for those noble truths.

Blessed One, how much could one possibly proclaim of the qualities of the four meditative absorptions? For the qualities of the meditative absorptions are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for those meditative absorptions.”

“Blessed One, how much can be proclaimed of the qualities of the four immeasurables? For the qualities of the immeasurables are indeed immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for them. Blessed One, how much can be proclaimed of the qualities of the four formless attainments? For the qualities of the formless attainments are indeed immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for them.”

“Blessed One, how much can be said in praise of the qualities of the eight liberations? For the qualities of the liberations are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for those liberations.

Blessed One, how much can be said in praise of the qualities of the nine successive meditative attainments? For the qualities of the successive meditative attainments are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for those successive meditative attainments.”
"Blessed One, how many virtues of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—can be proclaimed?

For the virtues of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are indeed immeasurable. And those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for these gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness."

"How many, O Blessed One, can the qualities of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) be proclaimed? For the qualities of the superknowledges are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for those superknowledges.

How many, O Blessed One, can the qualities of the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) be proclaimed? For the qualities of the meditative absorptions are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for those meditative absorptions."

“Blessed One, how much is it possible to proclaim the qualities of the gateways of the dhāraṇīs? For the qualities of the gateways of the dhāraṇīs are immeasurable; and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for those gateways of the dhāraṇīs.

Blessed One, how much is it possible to proclaim the qualities of the ten powers of a Tathāgata? For the qualities of the powers of a Tathāgata are immeasurable; and these relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for those powers of a Tathāgata.”

“Blessed One, how much can be said regarding the qualities of the four grounds of self-confidence? For the qualities of the grounds of self-confidence are indeed immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are themselves the grounds of self-confidence.

Blessed One, how much can be said regarding the qualities of the four analytical knowledges? For the qualities of the analytical knowledges are indeed immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are themselves the analytical knowledges.”

“Blessed One, how many qualities of great loving-kindness can be proclaimed? For the qualities of great loving-kindness are indeed immeasurable; and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for that great loving-kindness. Blessed One, how many qualities of great compassion can be proclaimed? For the qualities of great compassion are indeed immeasurable; and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for that great compassion.”

"To what extent, Blessed One, can the qualities of the eighteen unique attributes of a Buddha be proclaimed? For the qualities of the eighteen unique attributes of a Buddha are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for these unique attributes of a Buddha. To what extent, Blessed One, can the qualities of omniscience be proclaimed? For the qualities of omniscience are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for that omniscience."

"To what extent, Blessed One, can the qualities of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) be proclaimed? For the qualities of the knowledge of the aspects of the path are indeed immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for that knowledge of the aspects of the path.

To what extent, Blessed One, can the qualities of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) be proclaimed? For the qualities of the knowledge of all aspects are indeed immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are [the vessel] for that knowledge of all aspects."

“Blessed One, how many qualities of suchness can be proclaimed? For the qualities of suchness are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for that suchness. Blessed One, how many qualities of non-falsity can be proclaimed? For the qualities of non-falsity are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for that non-falsity.”

“Blessed One, how many qualities of non-dual suchness can be proclaimed? For the qualities of non-dual suchness are indeed immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for that non-dual suchness. Blessed One, how many qualities of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) can be proclaimed? For the qualities of the nature of phenomena are indeed immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for that nature of phenomena.”

“Blessed One, how many qualities of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) can be proclaimed? For the qualities of the dharma-realm are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for the dharma-realm. Blessed One, how many qualities of the stability of phenomena (dharmasthititā) can be proclaimed? For the qualities of the stability of phenomena are immeasurable, and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for the stability of phenomena.”

"To what extent, Blessed One, can the qualities of the fixed order of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*) be proclaimed? For the qualities of the fixed order of phenomena are indeed immeasurable; and those relics of the Tathāgata are the very essence of that fixed order of phenomena.

To what extent, Blessed One, can the qualities of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) be proclaimed? For the qualities of the limit of reality are indeed immeasurable; and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for that limit of reality."

"Blessed One, how many qualities of the inconceivable realm can be proclaimed? For the qualities of the inconceivable realm are indeed immeasurable; and those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for that inconceivable realm.

Blessed One, how many qualities of the abandonment of all afflictions along with their latencies and habitual tendencies can be proclaimed? For the qualities of the abandonment of all afflictions along with their latencies and habitual tendencies are indeed immeasurable."

And those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel. O Blessed One, how many virtues of dwelling in equanimity can be proclaimed? For the virtues of dwelling in equanimity are indeed immeasurable; and it is because of dwelling in equanimity that those relics of the Tathāgata are [the vessel].

O Blessed One, how many virtues of the nature of non-forgetfulness can be proclaimed? For the virtues of the nature of non-forgetfulness are indeed immeasurable; and it is because of the nature of non-forgetfulness that those relics of the Tathāgata are [the vessel].
Therefore those relics of the Tathāgata receive worship;
O Blessed One, because those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for the perfection of jewels, they therefore receive worship.
“Blessed One, those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for the perfection of neither affliction nor purification;
therefore, those relics of the Tathāgata receive worship because of the perfection of non-arising and non-ceasing.”
"Blessed One, those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel;
it is because of that that those relics of the Tathāgata receive worship.
Blessed One, those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for the perfection of non-undertaking and non-abandonment."
Therefore those relics of the Tathāgata receive worship;
because, O Blessed One, those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for the perfection of neither adding nor subtracting,
therefore those relics of the Tathāgata receive worship.
"Blessed One, those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for the perfection of non-coming, non-going, and non-abiding;
therefore, those relics of the Tathāgata receive worship.
Blessed One, those relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for the perfection of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)."

And because those relics of the Tathāgata have been permeated by that perfection of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-pāramitā*), those relics of the Tathāgata receive worship even after that Tathāgata has entered final nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Blessed One, let alone the relics of the Tathāgata filling the crevices of a single three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system; [let alone those filling all such systems].

If, Blessed One, world-systems in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā were filled with the relics of the Tathāgata, bound together like a crest-ornament, and there were also this book of the Perfection of Wisdom—of these two items, Blessed One, I would take this very Perfection of Wisdom. Why is that?

Because, Blessed One, it is from this [Perfection of Wisdom] that those relics of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, have emerged; for it is because they have been permeated by the Perfection of Wisdom, Blessed One, that those relics are honored.
The relics of the Tathāgata receive worship. Furthermore, Bhagavān,

if a son of good family or a daughter of good family should honor, revere, respect, and worship the relics of the Tathāgata, they will, upon reaching the limit of that root of merit, experience the prosperity of gods and humans.

Having experienced happiness among the great kṣatriya families, the great brāhmaṇa families, and the great householder families, and among the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, he will, by that very root of merit, bring an end to suffering.
Such is the fruit of making offerings to the relics of the Tathāgata; furthermore, by taking up, retaining, reciting, mastering, and properly attending to this Perfection of Wisdom,
they will fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration and they will fulfill the perfection of vigor.
They will fulfill the perfection of patience, they will fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline,
and they will fulfill the perfection of generosity.
He will fulfill internal emptiness, he will fulfill external emptiness,
and he will fulfill internal-external emptiness.
He will fulfill the emptiness of emptiness, he will fulfill the great emptiness,
and he will fulfill the emptiness of the ultimate truth.
He will fulfill the emptiness of the conditioned, he will fulfill the emptiness of the unconditioned,
and he will fulfill absolute emptiness.
He will fulfill the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end; he will fulfill the emptiness of non-dispersal;
he will fulfill the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
He will fulfill the emptiness of all phenomena, he will fulfill the emptiness of specific characteristics,
and he will fulfill the emptiness of non-apprehension.
He will fulfill the emptiness of non-existence,
he will fulfill the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and he will fulfill the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
He will fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness,
he will fulfill the four right efforts,
and he will fulfill the four bases of miraculous power.
He will fulfill the five faculties, he will fulfill the five powers,
and he will fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment.
He will fulfill the noble eightfold path; he will fulfill the four noble truths,
he will fulfill the four meditative absorptions,
and he will fulfill the four immeasurables.
He will fulfill the four formless attainments,
he will fulfill the eight liberations,
and he will fulfill the nine successive meditative attainments.
He will fulfill the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; he will fulfill the five supernormal knowledges;
he will fulfill the meditative concentrations.
He will fulfill the gateways of dhāraṇī;
he will fulfill the ten powers of a Tathāgata; he will fulfill the four grounds of self-confidence.
He will fulfill the four analytical knowledges; he will fulfill great loving-kindness;
he will fulfill great compassion.
He will fulfill the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Having transcended the level of the śrāvaka and the level of the pratyekabuddha, he will enter the fixed course of a bodhisattva;
having entered the fixed course of a bodhisattva, he will attain the superknowledges of a bodhisattva.
Having attained the superknowledges of a bodhisattva, he will travel from buddha-field to buddha-field;
he will intentionally assume a physical form by means of which the maturation of sentient beings will occur.

Whether in the form of a universal monarch, or in the great kṣatriya clans, or in the great brahmin clans, or in the great householder clans, or in the form of Śakra, or in the form of Brahmā, or in the form of Vaiśravaṇa— he will bring sentient beings to maturity through those various embodiments.

Therefore, Blessed One, it is not that I lack respect for the bodies of the Tathāgatas, nor do I lack confidence in them, nor am I unwilling to worship them, nor am I unwilling to receive them. Rather, Blessed One, when a son of good family or a daughter of good family honors, reveres, respects, and worships this perfection of wisdom, they have thereby accumulated the cause for all the Buddha-qualities and all forms of prosperity.
And they become embraced [by the Buddhas], and the relics of the Tathāgatas become honored, revered, and worshipped.
Furthermore, Blessed One, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who exist in the ten directions...

Desiring to see, with both the Dharma-body and the Wisdom-body, those [Buddhas] who abide, remain, and maintain themselves in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems, teaching the Dharma; and desiring to worship them, this Perfection of Wisdom should be taken up,
retained, recited, mastered, worshipped, and extensively proclaimed to others.
And they should attend to them with wise reflection;

that son of good family or daughter of good family will behold those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems in the ten directions. In this way, indeed, by that son of good family or daughter of good family...
And that mindfulness of those Buddhas should be cultivated within the perfection of wisdom by way of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Furthermore, Blessed One, a son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to behold those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, should take up, retain, and recite this perfection of wisdom.
It should be mastered, set in motion, honored, extensively proclaimed to others, and properly attended to with right reflection;
for, O Blessed One, regarding the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), there are these two natures of phenomena.
Which two? The conditioned nature of phenomena and the unconditioned nature of phenomena.
And what, Blessed One, is the conditioned nature of phenomena?
It is the knowledge of internal emptiness, the knowledge of external emptiness, and the knowledge of internal and external emptiness.

The knowledge that exists in the emptiness of emptiness; the knowledge that exists in the great emptiness; the knowledge that exists in the emptiness of the ultimate; the knowledge that exists in the emptiness of the conditioned; the knowledge that exists in the emptiness of the unconditioned; the knowledge that exists in the absolute emptiness;

the knowledge that exists in the emptiness of the beginningless and endless; the knowledge that exists in the emptiness of non-dispersal; and the knowledge that exists in the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

It is the knowledge of the emptiness of all phenomena; it is the knowledge of the emptiness of specific characteristics; it is the knowledge of the emptiness of non-apprehension; it is the knowledge of the emptiness of non-existence; it is the knowledge of the emptiness of intrinsic nature; it is the knowledge of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;
and it is the knowledge regarding the four applications of mindfulness.
The knowledge regarding the four right efforts,
the knowledge regarding the four bases of psychic power,
and the knowledge regarding the five faculties.
That which is knowledge regarding the five powers, that which is knowledge regarding the seven factors of enlightenment,
and that which is knowledge regarding the noble eightfold path.
The knowledge regarding the four noble truths, the knowledge regarding the four meditative absorptions, and the knowledge regarding the four immeasurables.
That which is knowledge regarding the four formless attainments,
that which is knowledge regarding the eight liberations, and that which is knowledge regarding the nine successive meditative attainments;

That which is knowledge regarding the doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; that which is knowledge regarding the five superknowledges; and that which is knowledge regarding all meditative concentrations.
The knowledge that exists in all the gateways of dhāraṇī,
the knowledge that exists in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and the knowledge that exists in the four grounds of self-confidence;
That which is the knowledge regarding the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), that which is the knowledge regarding great loving-kindness (mahāmaitrī),
and that which is the knowledge regarding great compassion (mahākaruṇā).
That which is knowledge regarding the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
that which is knowledge regarding wholesome phenomena; and that which is knowledge regarding unwholesome phenomena.
That which is knowledge regarding phenomena with outflows, that which is knowledge regarding phenomena without outflows,
and that which is knowledge regarding mundane phenomena.
That which is the knowledge regarding supramundane phenomena is called the true nature (*dharmatā*) of conditioned phenomena.
In that regard, what is the true nature of unconditioned phenomena?

That which has no arising, no cessation, no staying, no duration, no alteration, no defilement, no purification, no decrease, and no increase—this is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāvatā*) of all phenomena.
And what is this intrinsic nature of all phenomena?
It is said that all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature.
The true nature of unconditioned phenomena.
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Kauśika, so it is."
Those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones who existed in the past also awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment by relying on this very perfection of wisdom;
those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones who will exist in the future will also awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment by relying on this very perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones who currently reside, remain, and maintain themselves while teaching the Dharma in the immeasurable and incalculable world-systems of the ten directions—
they too, by relying on this very perfection of wisdom, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
And those who were the disciples of the past Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones—

Those who will be the disciples of the future Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, as well as those who are now the disciples of the present Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones— they too, by relying on this very perfection of wisdom, have attained, will attain, and are attaining the fruit of stream-entry.
They have attained, will attain, and are attaining the fruit of once-returning;
they have attained, will attain, and are attaining the fruit of non-returning;
they have attained, will attain, and are attaining arhatship.
Those who were Pratyekabuddhas in the past,
those who will be Pratyekabuddhas in the future,
and those Pratyekabuddhas who currently reside and remain in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems right now— [all these are sustained by this perfection of wisdom].
By means of these [teachings] as well, relying upon this very perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they have attained, will attain, and are attaining pratyekabodhi. For what reason?
Because herein, within this perfection of wisdom, all three vehicles are taught in detail.

Furthermore, these are by way of the yoga of signlessness, the yoga of non-apprehension, the yoga of non-arising, the yoga of non-ceasing, the yoga of non-defilement, the yoga of non-purification, the yoga of non-conditioning, the yoga of non-accumulation, the yoga of non-dispersal, the yoga of non-addition, the yoga of non-subtraction, the yoga of non-grasping, and the yoga of non-abandonment;
yet that is according to worldly convention and not in the ultimate sense. Why is that?
Because the perfection of wisdom is neither a shore nor a non-shore; for the perfection of wisdom is neither the near shore nor the far shore.

It is neither high nor low, neither level nor uneven, neither with signs nor signless, neither mundane nor supramundane, neither conditioned nor unconditioned, neither wholesome nor unwholesome, neither past nor future nor present; for indeed, Kauśika, the perfection of wisdom is not the giver of the Buddha-dharmas.

For indeed, Kauśika, the perfection of wisdom is not the giver of the qualities of a stream-enterer; for indeed, Kauśika, the perfection of wisdom is not the giver of the qualities of a once-returner;
for indeed, Kauśika, the perfection of wisdom is not the giver of the qualities of a non-returner.
For indeed, Kauśika, the perfection of wisdom is not the giver of the dharmas of an Arhat; for indeed, Kauśika, the perfection of wisdom is not the giver of the dharmas of a Pratyekabuddha;
for indeed, Kauśika, the perfection of wisdom is not the giver of the dharmas of an ordinary person.
Śakra said: "O Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is a great perfection;

for herein, O Blessed One, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom thoroughly understand the mental activities of all sentient beings, yet they do not apprehend a sentient being, nor do they apprehend the designation 'sentient being,' nor do they apprehend a self."

One does not perceive a being, one does not perceive a soul, one does not perceive a creature, one does not perceive a person, one does not perceive an individual, one does not perceive a human, one does not perceive a youth, one does not perceive an agent, one does not perceive an experiencer, one does not perceive a knower, and one does not perceive a seer.
One does not perceive form,
one does not perceive feeling, one does not perceive perception.
He does not perceive volitional formations;
he does not perceive consciousness.
He does not perceive the eye.
He does not perceive the ear, he does not perceive the nose,
he does not perceive the tongue.
He does not apprehend the body,
he does not apprehend the mind;
he does not apprehend form.
One does not perceive sound,
one does not perceive odor,
and one does not perceive taste.
One does not perceive contact, nor does one perceive mental phenomena.
One does not perceive visual consciousness.
He does not perceive ear-consciousness,
he does not perceive nose-consciousness,
he does not perceive tongue-consciousness.
One does not perceive body-consciousness,
nor does one perceive mind-consciousness.
One does not perceive eye-contact.
He does not perceive ear-contact, he does not perceive nose-contact,
he does not perceive tongue-contact.
One does not perceive body-contact,
nor does one perceive mind-contact.
One does not perceive the feeling conditioned by eye-contact.
One does not apprehend feeling conditioned by ear-contact;
one does not apprehend feeling conditioned by nose-contact;
one does not apprehend feeling conditioned by tongue-contact.
One does not perceive feeling conditioned by bodily contact, nor does one perceive feeling conditioned by mental contact.
One does not perceive the earth element.
One does not apprehend the water element, one does not apprehend the fire element, and one does not apprehend the wind element.
One does not perceive the element of space,
nor does one perceive the element of consciousness.
One does not perceive ignorance.
He does not perceive volitional formations,
he does not perceive consciousness,
and he does not perceive name-and-form.
One does not perceive the six sense bases,
one does not perceive contact,
and one does not perceive feeling.
One does not perceive craving,
one does not perceive grasping,
and one does not perceive existence.
One does not perceive birth,
nor does one perceive old age and death.
One does not perceive the perfection of generosity.
He does not apprehend the perfection of ethical discipline,
he does not apprehend the perfection of patience,
and he does not apprehend the perfection of vigor.
He does not apprehend the perfection of meditation,
nor does he apprehend the perfection of wisdom.
He does not apprehend internal emptiness.
He does not apprehend external emptiness,
nor does he apprehend internal-external emptiness,
nor does he apprehend the emptiness of emptiness.
He does not perceive great emptiness, he does not perceive ultimate emptiness,
and he does not perceive conditioned emptiness.
He does not perceive the emptiness of the unconditioned,
he does not perceive absolute emptiness,
and he does not perceive the emptiness of that which has neither beginning nor end.
He does not perceive the emptiness of non-dispersal, he does not perceive the emptiness of intrinsic nature,
and he does not perceive the emptiness of all phenomena.
He does not perceive the emptiness of specific characteristics, he does not perceive the emptiness of non-perception,
and he does not perceive the emptiness of non-existence.
One does not perceive the emptiness of intrinsic nature,
nor does one perceive the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
One does not perceive the applications of mindfulness.
They do not apprehend the right efforts, they do not apprehend the bases of psychic power, and they do not apprehend the faculties.
They do not apprehend the powers,
they do not apprehend the factors of enlightenment, and they do not apprehend the noble eightfold path.
They do not apprehend the noble truths; they do not apprehend the meditative concentrations; they do not apprehend the immeasurables.
They do not perceive the formless attainments; they do not perceive the eight liberations; they do not perceive the nine successive meditative attainments.
They do not apprehend the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they do not apprehend the superknowledges; they do not apprehend the meditative concentrations.
They do not apprehend the gateways of dhāraṇī;
they do not apprehend the ten powers of a Tathāgata; they do not apprehend the grounds of self-confidence.
They do not apprehend the analytical knowledges;
they do not apprehend great loving-kindness;
they do not apprehend great compassion.
They do not perceive the unique qualities of a Buddha,
nor do they perceive the fruit of stream-entry, nor the fruit of once-returning.
They do not apprehend [it], they do not apprehend the fruit of a non-returner, and they do not apprehend arhatship.
They do not apprehend the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
they do not apprehend the knowledge of the aspects of the path; they do not apprehend the knowledge of all aspects.
They do not perceive a bodhisattva, they do not perceive a Buddha,
and they do not perceive the qualities of a Buddha.
For the perfection of wisdom does not appear by way of apprehension. Why is that?
Because its intrinsic nature does not exist—that by which one might apprehend, that which might be apprehended, or wherein one might apprehend.
The Blessed One said:

"So it is, Kauśika, so it is. For when a bodhisattva mahāsattva has practiced the perfection of wisdom for a long time through the yoga of non-apprehension, he does not apprehend even awakening, let alone a Buddha."
[He practices] thus with respect to the Buddha-qualities.
Śakra said: "Furthermore, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice only in the perfection of wisdom and not in the other perfections?
The Blessed One said:
Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in all six perfections by way of non-apprehension. He does not apprehend the gift, he does not apprehend the giver, nor does he apprehend the recipient;
he does not apprehend morality, he does not apprehend one who possesses morality, nor does he apprehend immorality.
He does not apprehend patience, nor does he apprehend the patient one, nor does he apprehend malice;
he does not apprehend vigor, nor does he apprehend the vigorous one, nor does he apprehend laziness;
he does not apprehend meditative concentration, nor does he apprehend the meditator, nor does he apprehend distraction.
He does not apprehend wisdom, nor does he apprehend one possessed of wisdom, nor does he apprehend faulty wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva giving a gift in order to fulfill the perfection of generosity, it is the perfection of wisdom that is the precursor;
for a bodhisattva mahāsattva guarding his morality in order to fulfill the perfection of morality, it is the perfection of wisdom alone that is the precursor.
The perfection of wisdom alone is the precursor for a bodhisattva mahāsattva in order to accomplish patience and fulfill the perfection of patience;
the perfection of wisdom alone is the precursor for a bodhisattva mahāsattva when exerting vigor in order to fulfill the perfection of vigor;
the perfection of wisdom alone is the precursor for a bodhisattva mahāsattva when entering the meditative absorptions in order to fulfill the perfection of meditation.

The perfection of wisdom itself is the precursor for a bodhisattva mahāsattva in order to fulfill the perfection of wisdom through the seclusion of all phenomena by means of the yoga of non-apprehension of all phenomena. This is by means of the non-apprehension of form, by means of the non-apprehension of feeling, and by means of the non-apprehension of perception. (ŚsP_II-4_120)
By way of non-apprehension,
by way of the non-apprehension of formative forces,
and by way of the non-apprehension of consciousness.
By way of the non-apprehension of the eye, by way of the non-apprehension of the ear,
and by way of the non-apprehension of the nose.
By way of the non-apprehension of the tongue,
by way of the non-apprehension of the body, and by way of the non-apprehension of the mind.
By way of the non-apprehension of form,
by way of the non-apprehension of sound,
and by way of the non-apprehension of odor.
by way of the non-apprehension of taste, by way of the non-apprehension of touch,
and by way of the non-apprehension of phenomena.
By way of the non-apprehension of eye-consciousness, by way of the non-apprehension of ear-consciousness,
and by way of the non-apprehension of nose-consciousness.
By way of the non-apprehension of tongue-consciousness,
by way of the non-apprehension of body-consciousness, and by way of the non-apprehension of mind-consciousness.
By way of the non-apprehension of eye-contact, by way of the non-apprehension of ear-contact,
and by way of the non-apprehension of nose-contact.
By way of the non-apprehension of tongue-contact,
by way of the non-apprehension of body-contact, and by way of the non-apprehension of mind-contact.
By way of the non-apprehension of feeling born of eye-contact, by way of the non-apprehension of feeling born of ear-contact,
and by way of the non-apprehension of feeling born of nose-contact.
By means of the non-apprehension of feeling born of tongue-contact,
by means of the non-apprehension of feeling born of body-contact, and by means of the non-apprehension of feeling born of mind-contact.
By way of the non-apprehension of the earth element, by way of the non-apprehension of the water element,
and by way of the non-apprehension of the fire element.
By way of the non-apprehension of the element of wind,
by way of the non-apprehension of the element of space, and by way of the non-apprehension of the element of consciousness.
by way of the non-apprehension of ignorance,
by way of the non-apprehension of formative forces,
and by way of the non-apprehension of consciousness;
by way of the non-apprehension of name-and-form, by way of the non-apprehension of the six sense bases,
and by way of the non-apprehension of contact;
by way of the non-apprehension of sensation, by way of the non-apprehension of craving,
and by way of the non-apprehension of grasping;
By way of the non-apprehension of existence,
by way of the non-apprehension of birth, and by way of the non-apprehension of old age and death.
by way of the non-apprehension of the perfection of generosity, by way of the non-apprehension of the perfection of ethical discipline,
and by way of the non-apprehension of the perfection of patience;
By means of the yoga of non-apprehension of the perfection of vigor, by means of the yoga of non-apprehension of the perfection of meditation,
and by means of the yoga of non-apprehension of the perfection of wisdom.
By means of the non-apprehension of internal emptiness,
by means of the non-apprehension of external emptiness,
and by means of the non-apprehension of internal-external emptiness.
by means of the non-apprehension of the emptiness of emptiness, by means of the non-apprehension of great emptiness,
and by means of the non-apprehension of the emptiness of the ultimate;
By means of the non-apprehension of conditioned emptiness,
by means of the non-apprehension of unconditioned emptiness,
and by means of the non-apprehension of absolute emptiness.
by means of the non-apprehension of the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end,
by means of the non-apprehension of the emptiness of non-dispersal,
and by means of the non-apprehension of the emptiness of intrinsic nature;
by means of the non-apprehension of the emptiness of all phenomena, by means of the non-apprehension of the emptiness of specific characteristics,
and by means of the non-apprehension of the emptiness of non-apprehension;
By means of the non-apprehension of the emptiness of non-existence,
by means of the non-apprehension of the emptiness of intrinsic nature,
and by means of the non-apprehension of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
By way of the non-apprehension of the four foundations of mindfulness, by way of the non-apprehension of the four right efforts,
and by way of the non-apprehension of the four bases of psychic power;
by way of the non-apprehension of the five faculties, by way of the non-apprehension of the five powers,
and by way of the non-apprehension of the seven factors of enlightenment;
by way of the non-apprehension of the noble eightfold path, by way of the non-apprehension of the four noble truths,
and by way of the non-apprehension of the four meditative absorptions;
by way of the non-apprehension of the four immeasurables, by way of the non-apprehension of the four formless attainments,
and by way of the non-apprehension of the eight liberations;

By means of the yoga of non-apprehension of the nine successive meditative attainments; by means of the yoga of non-apprehension of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
by means of the yoga of non-apprehension of the five superknowledges;
and by means of the yoga of non-apprehension of all meditative concentrations.
By way of the non-apprehension of all the gateways of dhāraṇī, by way of the non-apprehension of the ten powers of a Tathāgata,
and by way of the non-apprehension of the four grounds of self-confidence;
by way of the non-apprehension of the four analytical knowledges, by way of the non-apprehension of great loving-kindness,
and by way of the non-apprehension of great compassion;
by way of the non-apprehension of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, by way of the non-apprehension of the fruit of stream-entry,
and by way of the non-apprehension of the fruit of once-returning;
by way of the non-apprehension of the fruit of non-returning, by way of the non-apprehension of arhatship, and by way of the non-apprehension of individual enlightenment;
by way of the non-apprehension of the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and by way of the non-apprehension of the knowledge of all aspects.

Kauśika, it is just as, for example, there is no distinction in the shadow cast by the trees of Jambudvīpa, though they have various leaves, various flowers, various fruits, various numbers, and various heights and girths.

Or rather, no distinction or difference is perceived; they are merely designated by the number "shadows, shadows. In the same way, Kauśika, when the five perfections are embraced by the perfection of wisdom and dedicated toward the knowledge of omniscience, no distinction or difference is perceived.
Śakra said: "Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is endowed with great qualities; it fulfills all qualities.
Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is endowed with immeasurable qualities, endowed with infinite qualities, and endowed with boundless qualities."

Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is endowed with qualities that are without end; for, Blessed One, if some son of good family or daughter of good family were to write down this perfection of wisdom, make it into a book, and preserve it, and honor, revere, respect, and worship it with flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, and powders.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to honor [the Buddha] with robes, parasols, banners, flags, and various musical instruments, and furthermore, were to attend to the Perfection of Wisdom as it has been taught in a systematic manner; and if another son of good family or daughter of good family were to take this Perfection of Wisdom,
having placed it in a book, and give it to someone else— of these two, which one would generate the greater merit?
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, Kauśika, I shall question you on this matter;
answer as you see fit. What do you think?"

Kauśika, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family should honor, revere, respect, and worship the relics of the Tathāgata with flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, flags, and various kinds of musical instruments;

And if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to give even a relic of the Tathāgata the size of a mustard seed to another, sharing it with them, that son of good family or daughter of good family,

having taken that relic of the Tathāgata the size of a mustard seed, would honor, revere, respect, and worship it with flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags.
and with various musical instruments—of these two, which would produce the greater merit?
Śakra said: "As I understand the meaning of what has been spoken by the Blessed One, O Blessed One,"

If any son of good family or daughter of good family should honor, revere, respect, and worship the relics of the Tathāgata with flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and various kinds of musical instruments;
Whoever should give even a mustard-seed-sized relic of the Tathāgata to another would generate much more merit than that; it was with this very purpose in mind, O Blessed One, that the Tathāgata,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, having entered the diamond-like samādhi, [attained] a diamond-like physical body.

Having broken open the consecrated relics of the Tathāgata and generated great compassion for the bodies of sentient beings—[for the sake] of those beings who are to be disciplined by the Tathāgata-element—he asked:
"For what reason?
Blessed One, whoever shall worship even a relic of the Tathāgata as small as a mustard seed with various kinds of offerings, they shall all [reach] the limit of that root of merit."
"Having attained it, they will bring an end to suffering.
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Kauśika, so it is."

For any son of good family or daughter of good family, Kauśika, who, having made this perfection of wisdom into a book, should honor, revere, respect, and worship it with flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes,
umbrellas, banners, flags, and various kinds of musical instruments— and [who likewise honors] this perfection of wisdom...
Having written it out for another and given it to them out of love for the Dharma, that son of good family or daughter of good family would generate much more merit.
Furthermore, Kauśika, whichever son of good family or daughter of good family [takes up] this perfection of wisdom as it has been taught...
Having gone to others, one should tell them, teach them, proclaim them, circulate them, analyze them, and clarify them;

this son of good family or daughter of good family would generate much more merit than those previous sons of good family or daughters of good family. They should be regarded as the Teacher himself, or as any other wise fellow-practitioner who occupies a position of authority. Why is that?

In this regard, Kauśika, this very Prajñāpāramitā is the Teacher; for there is no Teacher other than the Prajñāpāramitā, nor is the Prajñāpāramitā anything other than the Teacher—the Prajñāpāramitā itself is the Teacher, and the Teacher is the Prajñāpāramitā. Why is that?

Because it is by training in this Prajñāpāramitā that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present have awakened, do awaken, and will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Even those wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life are none other than irreversible bodhisattvas,

having trained in this perfection of wisdom, who have awakened, are awakening, and will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. For it is in this perfection of wisdom, Kauśika, that even those belonging to the vehicle of the disciples (śrāvakayānika) have trained.
They have attained, are attaining, and will attain the fruit of stream-entry;
they have attained, are attaining, and will attain the fruit of once-returning;
they have attained, are attaining, and will attain the fruit of non-returning.
Those who have attained, are attaining, and will attain arhatship;
those belonging to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas who, having trained, have awakened, are awakening, and will awaken to pratyekabodhi;
and even the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, who, having trained, have entered, are entering, and will enter the fixed course of a bodhisattva.
[They] have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; they have fully awakened, and they will fully awaken.

Therefore, Kausika, sons of good family or daughters of good family who desire to honor, revere, respect, and worship the Tathagatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones with their own faces [should do so] with flowers and garlands.

With perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and various musical instruments, this very perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) should be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped with flowers,

garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and various musical instruments; for, perceiving this very purpose, [one seeks] unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi).
After he had attained full awakening, this thought occurred to him:

"Toward whom should I dwell having paid honor, shown reverence, offered respect, and performed worship, relying upon them as my support? Then, Kauśika, in this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, its gods, humans, and asuras—[he considered: "Who is there?"
I did not perceive anyone who was my equal or my superior;
then this thought occurred to me:
"What if I were to honor and revere that very Dharma which I have fully awakened to—tranquil and sublime?"
Having honored, worshipped, and relied upon it, I would dwell; and what, Kauśika, is that dharma?
It is this very perfection of wisdom. I myself, Kauśika, first honor, revere, respect, and worship this perfection of wisdom;
having honored, revered, respected, and worshipped it, I dwell relying upon it.

How much more so, Kauśika, should a son of good family or a daughter of good family who desires to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment not honor, revere, respect, and worship this perfection of wisdom with flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and various kinds of musical instruments?

Kauśika, whether by sons of good family or daughters of good family belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, or even by sons of good family or daughters of good family belonging to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, this very perfection of wisdom should be honored,
revered, esteemed, and worshipped with flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, and parasols.

With banners, flags, and various musical instruments. For what reason? It is because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are produced from the perfection of wisdom; Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are produced from Bodhisattvas; and Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are produced from Tathāgatas. Therefore, O Kauśika, [it is so].

Noble sons or noble daughters belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, as well as noble sons or noble daughters belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, should honor, revere, respect, and worship this very Perfection of Wisdom with flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, and parasols.

With banners, flags, and various musical instruments—having trained in which, sons of good family and daughters of good family have awakened, are awakening, and will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and those belonging to the vehicle of the disciples have attained, are attaining, and will attain arhatship; and those belonging to the vehicle of the solitary buddhas have attained, are attaining, and will attain solitary enlightenment.
Those who have attained, those who are attaining, and those who will attain [the goal] do so by means of the Perfection of Wisdom in One Hundred Thousand Lines. This is the twenty-second chapter.
Then the Blessed One addressed Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"If, Kauśika, some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings of Jambudvīpa in the ten paths of wholesome action, what do you think, Kauśika?
Would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?"
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
The Blessed One said:

"Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family would generate much merit who would give a book of this perfection of wisdom to another for the purpose of reading or copying it."
Or for the sake of reciting it. For what reason?

Because herein, in this Perfection of Wisdom, the untainted dharmas are taught in detail; having trained in them, sons of good family and daughters of good family have entered, are entering, and will enter the fixed course of rightness.

Those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry, those who are attaining it, and those who will attain it; those who have attained the fruit of once-returning, those who are attaining it, and those who will attain it; those who have attained the fruit of non-returning, those who are attaining it, and those who will attain it.
They have attained, are attaining, and will attain arhatship;

those belonging to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas have attained, are attaining, and will attain pratyekabodhi; and those who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment have entered, are entering, and will enter the state of certainty in correctness.
They have awakened, are awakening, and will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
And what, Kauśika, are those impure dharmas taught in detail?

Namely: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.
emptiness of the internal,
emptiness of the external,
and emptiness of the internal and external;
emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness,
and emptiness of the ultimate truth;
emptiness of the conditioned, emptiness of the unconditioned,
and absolute emptiness;
emptiness without beginning or end, emptiness of non-dispersal,
and natural emptiness.
the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of specific characteristics,
and the emptiness of non-apprehension;
emptiness of non-existence,
emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

The eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, great compassion, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha— these, Kauśika, are the untainted dharmas taught through the perfection of wisdom, in which sons of good family and daughters of good family have trained, and by training in which they have awakened, are awakening, and will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

In this way, Kauśika, a son of good family or a daughter of good family would generate much more merit by establishing a single sentient being in the fruit of stream-entry than by establishing all the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa in the ten paths of wholesome action. Why is that?

Kauśika, when beings are established in the ten paths of wholesome action but are not yet liberated from the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama, they are thereby established in the fruit of stream-entry; Kauśika, those beings are liberated from the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama.
What need is there to mention one who would establish them in the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or in arhatship?
Furthermore, Kauśika, if someone were to establish all the beings of Jambudvīpa in the fruit of stream-entry, in the fruit of once-returning, and in the fruit of non-returning,
and another were to establish a single being in pratyekabodhi, the latter would produce far more merit than the former;
or if some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings of Jambudvīpa in pratyekabodhi.

And if some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish even a single sentient being in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, this person alone would produce far more merit. Why is that?
Because such a person is engaged in ensuring the non-interruption of the Buddha’s lineage.
Whoever establishes even a single sentient being in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—for what reason is that?
Because, Kauśika, the stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas are born from the Bodhisattva;
and because, Kauśika, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are born from the Bodhisattva. Therefore, by this, Kauśika...

It should be understood in this way by way of analogy: a bodhisattva also should be honored, revered, respected, and esteemed with flowers, incense, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags,
and various kinds of musical instruments.
Together with the world of gods, including Māra and the Śrāvakas and Brāhmaṇas, [the Buddha said]:

"Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings of Jambudvīpa in the ten paths of wholesome action. What do you think, Kauśika? Would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?"
He said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family would generate even more merit than that."
Whoever should give a book of this perfection of wisdom to another,

whether for the purpose of reading, writing, or reciting it— for what reason is that? Because herein, in this perfection of wisdom, the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) are taught in detail, wherein sons of good family and daughters of good family, having trained, have entered and are entering the fixed course of rightness (*samyaktva-nyāma*).
And they will enter [the path]; having attained the fruit of stream-entry, they have attained it and will attain it;
having attained the fruit of once-returning, they have attained it and will attain it.
Those who have attained, are attaining, and will attain the fruit of non-returning; those who have attained, are attaining, and will attain arhatship;
and those belonging to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas who have attained, are attaining, [and will attain] pratyekabodhi.

And these bodhisattva mahāsattvas will attain it; those who have entered, are entering, and will enter the bodhisattva-determination, as well as those who have awakened, are awakening, and will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

And what, Kauśika, are those untainted dharmas? Namely: the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom;
as well as internal emptiness and external emptiness.
internal and external emptiness,
the emptiness of emptiness,
and great emptiness.
emptiness of the ultimate truth, emptiness of the conditioned, and emptiness of the unconditioned;
absolute emptiness,
emptiness of that which is without beginning or end,
and emptiness of non-dispersal;
emptiness of intrinsic nature, emptiness of all phenomena, and emptiness of specific characteristics.
the emptiness of non-apprehension, the emptiness of non-existence,
and the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
The emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
The four foundations of mindfulness and the four right efforts.
The four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, and the five powers.
The seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the four noble truths, the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling,

the gateways to liberation consisting of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the six superknowledges, all samādhis, all dhāraṇī gateways, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, as well as other immeasurable qualities of a Buddha, have been taught.
Therefore, Kauśika, by this very method you should understand it thus:
if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having written the perfection of wisdom in a book, should give it to others for the purpose of reciting, copying, or reading it;
This very person would generate far more merit than that. Why is that?
Because here, Kauśika, in this Perfection of Wisdom, all dharmas are taught in detail—those by which the great kṣatriya clans are known, and the great brahmin clans are known.
